# Nonlinear optical responses of semiconducting graphene nanoribbons:

# Strong constraint from a hidden symmetry

Jiawei Ruan1,2,3, Weichen Tang1,2,Yang-Hao Chan4,5, Chen Hu1,2, Xiaoxun Gong1,2, and

Steven G. Louie1,2†

## Abstract:

Nonlinear optical (NLO) responses are powerful tools for probing material structures, as they are highly sensitive to spatial symmetries. For instance, it is well known that having inversion symmetry forbids even-order NLO effects. Here, we show that nonspatial symmetries can also significantly constrain NLO responses. In graphene nanoribbons (GNRs) with bipartite-lattice structures, we identify the approximate bipartite-lattice particle-hole (BLPH) symmetry strongly suppresses even-order NLO effects, even for systems with no inversion symmetry. Importantly, we demonstrate that this approximate symmetry enables the optical generation of nearly pure spin shift currents in ferromagnetic GNRs, with the charge shift currents strongly suppressed. The spin orientation of these photo-induced DC spin currents can be easily tuned by an external magnetic field, providing distinct advantages over previous schemes for generating pure spin shift currents in antiferromagnetic systems. We illustrate our findings using a recently synthesized ferromagnetic Janus GNR. Our results underscore the significance of an overlooked symmetry aspect of NLO responses and highlight magnetic GNRs as promising candidates for spintronic devices.

Main text:

Introduction. Nonlinear optical (NLO) effects have garnered significant attention for decades due to their many fascinating physical phenomena and broad technological applications [1,2]. In particular, their sensitivity to crystal symmetry makes NLO responses exceptional probes for studying the structural properties of crystalline, nanostructured, and twisted moiré materials [3]. It is well established that in centrosymmetric materials, even-order optical responses, such as second-harmonic generation (SHG) and the bulk photovoltaic effect (BPVE), are strictly forbidden, resulting in the characteristic even-odd feature in highharmonic generation (HHG) spectra [4]. The relationship between NLO susceptibility tensors and crystal symmetries has been thoroughly investigated [1]. However, the exploration of nonspace-group symmetries that arise from internal properties within a system and their impact on NLO responses remains largely unexplored, with only limited cases considered so far [5].

Recent advances in bottom-up molecular precursor techniques have enabled the atomically precise design of a wide variety of graphene nanoribbons (GNRs), including control over their widths and diverse edge shapes [6–15]. These structurally precise 1D materials are of particular interest due to their tunable electronic and magnetic properties [16,17], making them promising candidates for nanoscale electronics devices [18]. Very recently, researchers have discovered a new class of GNRs—Janus graphene nanoribbons (JGNRs)—characterized by two distinct edge terminations. Notably, these JGNRs exhibit intrinsic ferromagnetism, offering new possibilities for spin-based applications [19].

A common characteristic of GNRs is their honeycomb structure composed of carbon

atoms, with low-energy states predominantly derived from the 𝑝! orbitals. The next-nearestneighbor (NNN) hopping energies in GNRs are typically very small, an order of magnitude smaller compared to nearest-neighbor hopping energy. For GNRs in structures with only sixfold rings, if the NNN hoppings are neglected, the system can be regarded as in a bipartite lattice, in which the atomic sites are divided into two distinct sublattices, typically labeled A and B, such that each site in sublattice A is only interacting with sites in sublattice B, and vice versa. Such systems within the tight-binding formalism exhibit additional symmetries not explicitly given by the crystal space group, including chiral symmetry and particle-hole symmetry, with the latter being the combination of chiral and time-reversal (TR) symmetries [20]. Using chiral symmetry, a topological classification framework has been developed for the electronic structure of GNR systems [21].

In this work, we demonstrate that the particle-hole symmetry in a bipartite lattice system—referred to as bipartite-lattice particle-hole (BLPH) symmetry—strongly constrains NLO responses in semiconducting graphene nanoribbons. Based on bipartite-lattice models, we show that such symmetry prohibits any even-order NLO responses even in structures without inversion symmetry. For a real GNR with small NNN hoppings, the BLPH symmetry in the Bloch band states is slightly broken, but the system still strongly suppresses the even-

Furthermore, we show that in magnetic GNRs, although the chiral and TR symmetries are individually broken, their product, which leads to BLPH symmetry, remains approximately preserved. Taking the recently synthesized JGNR as a prototype material, we predict that this approximate symmetry enables optical generation of nearly pure spin shift currents in ferromagnetic GNRs, which is rarely achievable in conventional ferromagnetic materials. Our results underscore the significance of an overlooked symmetry aspect of NLO responses and position magnetic GNRs as compelling candidates for optospintronic technologies.

We note that in the literature, the phenomenon of light-induced counter-propagating electrons with opposite spin polarization through a second-order NLO process is referred to as the spin bulk photovoltaic (SBPV) effect. This phenomenon has long been pursued for its potential to generate spin currents in an ultrafast timescale while minimizing the drawbacks associated with charge currents [30]. Previously, the SBPV effect has been proposed in antiferromagnetic (AFM) systems [31–33]. However, the resulting spin polarization of the spin current depends on the orientation of AFM Neel order, which is difficult to control. In our


<!-- Page 7 -->


mechanism here, which arises from the BLPH symmetry, the photogeneration of nearly pure spin current can be achieved in a FM system. This makes the spin polarization of the spin current tunable by straightforwardly manipulating the direction of the magnetization of an FM sample with an external magnetic field (Fig. 3e). Moreover, by effectivity breaking the BLPH symmetry through mechanisms such as doping, the relative contributions of spin-up and spindown currents can be controlled on demand (see SM). These features suggest that JGNRs can be engineered to provide versatile spin sources for optospintronics and related applications.

Conclusions. We have discovered that the existence of an effective particle-hole symmetry in graphene nanoribbons with near bipartite lattice symmetry imposes formidable constraints on their NLO responses, strongly suppressing even-order NLO responses even in structures lacking inversion symmetry. Applying our theory to the recently synthesized Janus GNR, we predict that the approximate BLPH symmetry uniquely facilitates the optical generation of pure spin currents in a ferromagnetic system, with tunability via an external magnetic field. This finding offers new opportunities for high-performance optospintronics using magnetic GNRs. Moreover, the BLPH symmetry constraints on NLO responses are expected to apply broadly to other near bipartite lattice materials, regardless of their shape and dimensionality, such as the Lieb lattice and dice lattice [34], providing a fundamental and universal principle governing the optical activity in these systems.

## Abstract:

Graphene nanoribbons (GNRs) are a highly tunable class of one-dimensional (1D) quantum materials

that can be fabricated through bottom-up synthesis. Precise control over GNR band gaps and band-edge

alignments has established them as a promising nanoelectronics platform, but forming high-quality

electronic interfaces remains challenging. Here we combine sequential on-surface synthesis and scanning

tunneling microscopy (STM) induced dehydrogenation to directly write metallic 7-iGNR segments into

otherwise semiconducting H2-7-iGNRs without changing the GNR width or carbon backbone connectivity.

The resulting metallic segments exhibit nonzero spectral weight at the Fermi level (EF) and spatially

extended electronic states, consistent with two dispersive bands crossing EF. The new metallic states are

well-described by an extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger zigzag-ladder Hamiltonian. Scanning tunnelling

spectroscopy (STS) and first-principles calculations show that the valence band edge of adjacent, connected

semiconducting GNR segments lies close to EF for the metallic segments. STS spectra recover bulk GNR

properties within ~1 nm on either side of the metal-semiconductor GNR interface, with no discernable

depletion region. The observed GNR band edge alignment is consistent with a small energy barrier for hole

injection, thus suggesting a possible route towards atomically precise, low-barrier p-type contacts for future

GNR-based electronic devices.

## Introduction

Engineering the atomic structure of bottom-up-synthesized graphene nanoribbons (GNRs) is a

versatile strategy for tuning intrinsic GNR electronic properties since it allows experimental realization of

designer one-dimensional (1D) Hamiltonians.1-6 This has led to the production of ~1 nm width GNRs and

GNR heterostructures having a wide range of tunable semiconducting energy gaps.7-12 The incorporation of

GNRs into useful nanotechnological applications, however, has been hampered by difficulty in making

electrical contact between semiconducting GNRs and metallic electrodes due to the formation of large

Schottky barriers.13-19 One strategy for overcoming this problem is to create atomically-precise interfaces

between metallic and semiconducting GNR segments that allow GNR Schottky barriers to be tuned by

integrating bottom-up metallic contacts directly into single GNRs. Some progress has been made in this

direction through the linkage of semiconducting GNR segments having different widths and backbone

structures,20-26 as well as STM-based formation of semiconducting heterostructures directly within

individual GNRs.27 Two significant challenges that remain are, first, the creation of GNRs with broadly

dispersive metallic bands and, second, how to connect them seamlessly to semiconducting GNRs via

atomically-precise interface structures. The metallic GNRs made up to now have the disadvantage that they

are formed by daisy-chaining topological interface states28-30 that result in narrow bands that are vulnerable

to instabilities from strong interaction effects.29-31 No strategy has yet been shown that results in controllable,

seamless integration of metallic and semiconducting GNR segments from the bottom up. Overcoming these

challenges and developing a better understanding of GNR metal-semiconductor interfaces is essential for

realizing high-quality all-carbon contacts, interconnects, and logic elements for future nanoelectronics

applications.20-26,28,32

Here we demonstrate the synthesis of atomically-precise bottom-up GNRs that can be toggled from

an initial semiconducting state to a broadly dispersive two-channel metallic state through selective cleavage

of hydrogen atoms along its edges using STM tip manipulation. The ability to locally remove hydrogen

atoms allows metallic GNR segments to be directly written into otherwise semiconducting GNRs, enabling

controllable fabrication of bottom-up single-GNR metal-semiconductor heterojunctions that share a

common GNR backbone. STS measurements reveal that the characteristic bulk GNR electronic structures

of the two segments are recovered over a distance of only ~1 nm across the metal-semiconductor interface.

The dehydrogenated metallic state of this uniquely flexible GNR platform exhibits the electronic structure

of a nearly ideal quantum zigzag ladder (Figure 1a).33 In contrast, the presence of sp3-hybridized carbon

atoms (methylene groups) along fully hydrogenated edges of the GNR disrupts the extended carbon π-

electron network, thereby breaking its symmetry and leading to semiconducting GNR segments. This

behavior is seen in both our experimental STM measurements as well as in our theoretical DFT-based ab

initio simulations. Spatially-resolved spectroscopy of substrate-supported metal-semiconductor

heterojunctions additionally reveals valence band-edge alignment with the GNR Fermi level (EF) and no

resolvable extended depletion region. Such behavior is consistent with a small energy barrier for hole

injection, a property that is expected to be advantageous for producing low-resistance electrical contacts in

future GNR-based nanodevices.

broadly dispersive metallic bands requires reduced spacing between the orbitals to increase t1, but this also

increases the magnitude of NNN hopping t2. Such behavior is captured in the SSH Hamiltonian as follows:

A scheme for translating this model into the chemical structure of a 7-iGNR is illustrated in Figure 1b.

The 7-iGNR is closely related to the well-known 7-AGNR parent class assembled from anthracene building

blocks,1 but exhibits an alternating pattern of laterally fused benzo[f]isoindenyl groups along both edges.

We can gain insight into the electronic structure of 7-iGNRs through a defect model in which a single 6-

membered ring along the edge of a 7-AGNR is replaced by a 5-membered ring (Figure 1c). DFT simulation

of this scenario results in two defect states in the 7-AGNR energy gap that are split by ΔE ~ 0.4 eV (labeled

states 1 and 2 in Figure 1d). The wavefunctions for the two defect states are shown in Figure 1c and are

localized on the 5-membered ring, but exhibit orthogonal orbital symmetry. At charge neutrality the two

defect states accommodate three electrons with state 2 fully occupied and state 1 being only half filled

(Figure 1d). The electronic structure of the 7-iGNR shown in Figure 1b can be qualitatively thought of as a

periodic array of such defects. Here the two defect-derived states hybridize with neighboring cells and each

defect state forms a separate quantum zigzag ladder as described by Eq. (1). This hybridization broadens

the localized defect levels into two overlapping dispersive bands that cross EF, giving rise to a two-band

metallic electronic structure.

Surface-Assisted Growth of 7-iGNRs

Guided by this strategy, we designed a molecular precursor for the 7-iGNR, 9,9’-dibromo-2,2’,3,3’-

tetrahydro-1H,1’H-4,4’-bi(cyclopenta[b]naphthalene) (1) as shown in Figure 2a (molecular synthesis and

characterization are described in the Supplementary Information). Extended 7-iGNRs were prepared

following established surface-assisted bottom-up GNR growth protocols. 1 was first sublimed in ultrahigh

vacuum (UHV) from a Knudsen cell evaporator onto a clean Au(111) substrate held at T = 24 °C. Figure

2b shows a representative topographic STM image of a densely packed monolayer of 1 self-assembled into

a square lattice. On-surface step-growth polymerization of molecular precursors was induced by annealing

the molecule-decorated surface to T = 180 °C for 20 min. STM images of the resulting structures show

extended linear chains of poly-1 that laterally assemble into closely packed islands (Figure 2c). A second

annealing step at T = 300 °C (20 min) was performed to induce thermal cyclodehydrogenation, giving rise

to fully fused GNR backbones (Figure 2d). The positions and relative registry of the 5-membered rings are

encoded by precursor 1 and the geometry of Ullmann coupling, while cyclodehydrogenation primarily

forms the remaining 6-membered rings required to fuse the backbone. Bond-resolved STM (BRSTM)

imaging reveals periodic alternation of 5- and 6-membered rings lining the edges of the resulting GNRs

(Figure 2d). Throughout the growth irregular 5-ring sequences that result from the occasional flipping of a

benzo[f]isoindenyl group or incomplete cyclodehydrogenation represent the most common defects in H2-

7-iGNRs. In the following discussion we will focus on well-defined defect-free GNR segments whose

alternating 5-/6-membered-ring structure was directly verified by BRSTM (as seen in Figure 2d).

Based on the molecular design of 1 and the on-surface reaction sequence shown in Figure 2a, the as-

grown GNRs retain sp3 hybridized methylene (–CH2–) groups at the apex of the 5-membered-rings. This is

supported by topographic STM images that show the 5-membered rings as apparent depressions (~10 pm)

relative to 6-membered rings (Extended Data Fig. 1). We refer to this partially hydrogenated intermediate

GNR as H2-7-iGNR. The presence of methylene groups prevents the formation of the radical states

associated with the benzo[f]isoindenyl groups, effectively gapping out the metallic states expected for 7-

iGNRs and confining π-conjugation to the naphthalene cores along the H2-7-iGNR backbone.

To confirm this intuitive chemical picture we characterized the electronic structure of H2-7-iGNRs

using STS. Figure 3a shows a representative dI/dV point spectrum acquired above the position of a 5-

membered ring on as-grown H2-7-iGNR (dI/dV spectra reflect the local density of states (LDOS) under the

STM tip36). The two most prominent features bracketing EF are steep rises seen at Vs = +1.40 V (for

increasing Vs) (feature 1) and at Vs = –1.30 V (for decreasing Vs) (feature 3). Closer to EF we observe a third

(smaller) characteristic feature, a double peak centered at Vs = –0.20 V (feature 2). We assign feature 1 to

the H2-7-iGNR conduction band edge (CBE) and feature 2 to the H2-7-iGNR valence band edge (VBE).

From the positions of features 1 and 2 we extract an electronic bandgap Eg,exp = 1.6 ± 0.3 eV for H2-7-

iGNRs on Au(111). This is corroborated by dI/dV maps of H2-7-iGNR recorded over the range –0.20 V <

Vs < +1.40 V that show the featureless LDOS typically seen for semiconducting gaps (Extended Data Fig.

2).9 dI/dV maps recorded at biases corresponding to features 1, 2, and 3, on the other hand, show distinct

nodal patterns. Feature 1, for example, shows a faint brick-like pattern (Figure 3b) while features 2 and 3

show distinct striped patterns across the backbone of the GNR (Figures 3c,d). The bright protrusions seen

in feature 3 coincide with the positions of 6-membered rings lining the H2-7-iGNR edges (Figure 3d,

Extended Data Fig. 2).

These experimental features are consistent with ab initio DFT-LDA simulations of freestanding H2-7-

iGNRs (Figures 3e–i). Simulated H2-7-iGNR DOS (Figure 3h) and band structure (Figure 3i) both exhibit

a bandgap of 0.8 eV. Taking into account the well-known tendency of DFT-LDA to underestimate energy

gaps,7,8 the experimentally measured gap of 1.6 eV is in reasonable agreement with our DFT simulations.

The simulated LDOS maps (Figures 3e–g) also reasonably agree with the experimental dI/dV maps and

further support our assignment of features 1 and 2 to the CBE and VBE, respectively.

Tip-Induced Metallicity

Inspired by prior studies showing that H-atoms (e.g., methylene groups) lining the edges of

nanographenes (NGs) can be cleaved via STM tip manipulation,37-48 we sought to induce dehydrogenation

of H2-7-iGNRs into metallic 7-iGNRs by locally applying voltage pulses. Figure 2e shows the STM I–V

characteristic recorded while holding an STM tip ~5 Å above the edge of the H2-7-iGNR shown in Figure

2d (at the site of the red cross). As Vs is swept from 0 V to +2.5 V we observe a sudden drop in current at

VD ~ +2.3 V. This drop is irreversible, is independent of polarity, and appears only for voltages above a

threshold of |Vs| ≥ 2.0 V. Similar switching behavior has been observed for other NG systems and is known

to occur for tip-induced cleavage of C–H bonds.40,42,44

Low-bias BRSTM images recorded in the same region where tip manipulation has been performed

show amplitude modulation features commonly associated with the presence of electronic states very close

to EF—a hallmark of metallicity in GNRs (Figure 2f).29,30 Rather than being confined to the cleavage point

of a single C–H bond, however, these electronic states extend uniformly across the entire width of the ribbon

and ~2 nm along the length from the position of the tip during the pulse. Single voltage pulses thus appear

to cleave multiple C–H bonds, giving rise to metallic 7-iGNR segments centered at the position of the

applied tip-pulse. Analogous collective behavior has been observed in the decoupling of GNRs from

strongly interacting substrates, but is uncommon for tip-induced hydrogen abstraction.49 Such spatially

delocalized hydrogen removal may involve excitation through extended ribbon states followed by


<!-- Page 7 -->


7

vibrational-energy redistribution, or a short sequential cascade in which an initial dehydrogenation event

facilitates cleavage at neighboring methylene sites.

We characterized the electronic structure of 7-iGNRs obtained via tip-induced dehydrogenation by

recording dI/dV point spectra on GNR segments subjected to the tip manipulation protocol. Figure 3j shows

a representative dI/dV spectrum for a 7-iGNR obtained after tip-pulsing (our STS measurements focused

on 7-iGNR segments of length L ≳ 5nm to avoid confinement effects). Three prominent features unique to

7-iGNRs are observed: a broad peak at Vs = +0.80 V (feature 4), a narrower peak at Vs = +0.15 V (feature

5), and the onset of a shoulder at Vs = –1.20 V (feature 6). dI/dV maps recorded at a bias corresponding to

feature 4 show intensity patterns reminiscent of the zigzag ladder model of Figure 1a (Figure 3k). As bias

is decreased to feature 5 the dI/dV map evolves into a vertically striped phase that is modulated by a longer

wavelength along the ribbon axis (Figure 3l). The dI/dV intensity pattern at feature 6 exhibits diamond-

shaped structures at the positions of the 5-membered rings (Figure 3m). In contrast to the 1.6 ± 0.3 eV gap

observed for H2-7-iGNR, the activated 7-iGNR segments exhibit nonzero dI/dV intensity down to zero bias,

with no resolvable energy gap at EF. The diversity of nodal patterns spanning the range of –1.20 V < Vs <

+0.80 V for 7-iGNRs is consistent with an electronic structure in which more than one dispersive band

crosses EF (Extended Data Fig. 3).

Ab initio DFT-LDA simulations of 7-iGNRs help us to better understand the origin of metallicity in

this GNR. The band structure of a free-standing 7-iGNR is shown in Figure 3r and exhibits two highly

dispersive bands crossing EF (black lines) (charge density wave and magnetic ground states are ruled out at

the DFT-LDA level). These bands are degenerate at E–EF = –0.45 eV and give rise to a pair of van Hove

singularities (VHS1 and VHS2) that yield DOS peaks at E–EF = +0.33 eV and +0.80 eV (Figure 3q). A third

VHS at E–EF = –0.87 eV (VHS3) is seen at the bottom of the lower metallic band due to a gap arising from

an avoided crossing. Simulated 7-iGNR LDOS maps at energies corresponding to VHS1, VHS2, and VHS3

(Figures 3n–p) are in reasonably good agreement with the experimental dI/dV maps for features 4, 5, and 6

(Figures 3k–m), supporting the assignment of experimental features 4, 5 and 6 to van Hove singularities of

the 7-iGNR metallic band manifold. The calculated bandwidth from VHS1 to VHS3 (DEDFT ≈ 1.7 eV) also

reasonably matches the experimental bandwidth from feature 4 to feature 6 of 2.0 eV. Simulations of 7-

iGNR electronic structure that included the Au(111) substrate were also performed, leading to very similar

results.

We tested whether the 7-iGNR electronic structure can be quantitatively described as a quantum zigzag

ladder by performing a Wannier analysis of the Bloch states for the bands near EF obtained from our ab

initio DFT-LDA calculations. Such analysis is useful for determining the most appropriate tight-binding

model for a periodic system since it allows the ab initio Hamiltonian to be recast into a tight-binding form


<!-- Page 8 -->


8

with no adjustable parameters. To obtain maximally localized Wannier functions we found it necessary to

include the four 7-iGNR bands closest to EF. This procedure yields two Wannier functions per 5-membered

ring, analogous to the two defect states observed for a pristine 7-AGNR containing a single 5-membered

ring defect as shown in Figures 1c,d. By transforming the DFT Hamiltonian into the Wannier basis and

truncating small hopping terms we obtain an accurate tight-binding description with only NN and NNN

hopping terms, which corresponds precisely to the extended SSH Hamiltonian of Eq. (1) (see

Supplementary Information Note S1 for the full DFT Hamiltonian before truncation). Figure 1b shows the

two coexisting electronic networks associated with the two Wannier functions (Wannier states 1 and 2),

both of which resemble the zigzag ladder of Figure 1a and have the same orbital structure as the defect

states 1 and 2 in Figure 1c. The red lines in Figure 3r show the tight-binding band structure that results from

these two coexisting zigzag Wannier-function networks (Extended Data Table 1 shows the hopping

parameters for the truncated model). The two bands crossing EF thus arise from two zigzag ladder networks

and result in a two-band metallic electronic structure for 7-iGNRs. This makes 7-iGNRs a candidate two-

channel conductor and suggests that extended, low-disorder 7-iGNRs could support two independent

quantum conductance channels, analogous to metallic single-walled carbon nanotubes.50-53

Fabricating a Single-GNR Metal–Semiconductor Heterojunction

Having established that STM tip-induced dehydrogenation converts semiconducting H2-7-iGNRs into

metallic 7-iGNRs, we set out to explore the electronic properties of intra-ribbon metal-semiconductor

heterojunctions. Figure 4a shows a BRSTM image of a single GNR featuring a 2.5 nm long segment of

metallic 7-iGNR obtained by tip-pulsing embedded in an otherwise semiconducting H2-7-iGNR. The

detailed evolution of the electronic structure across a 7-iGNR/H2-7-iGNR metal-semiconductor interface

can be seen in Figure 4b. Here dI/dV is plotted as a function of Vs and position x across a single interface

(the vertical dashed line marks the location of the metal-semiconductor interface). At distances |x| > 1 nm

on either side of the interface the dI/dV spectra show characteristic features of the pristine H2-7-iGNR and

7-iGNR. The semiconducting VBE is observed to lie close to EF and no extended depletion region can be

resolved for the Au(111)-supported junction.

To gain a deeper understanding of the single-ribbon metal-semiconductor heterojunction behavior

observed here, we performed an ab initio DFT-LDA simulation of a freestanding 7-iGNR/H2-7-iGNR

structure as shown in Figure 4c (aimed at modeling the experiment shown in Figure 4b). Figure 4d shows

a plot of the resulting LDOS as a function of position and energy. At distances of |x| > 1 nm from the

interface the junction recovers the unperturbed electronic structure of pristine 7-iGNR and H2-7-iGNR,

showing signatures of van Hove singularities on the metallic side and band edge features on the

semiconducting side similar to the experiment. Our finite, freestanding junction simulation shows no


<!-- Page 9 -->


9

extended electrostatic variation, such as the signatures of electrostatic band-bending commonly seen for

macroscopic Schottky barriers. The simulation also shows no new states within the semiconducting H2-7-

iGNR gap near the interface. It is notable that EF for the metallic 7-iGNR segment in our simulation aligns

very closely with the VBE of the semiconducting H2-7-iGNR segment, similar to experiment, suggesting

that the freestanding junction model captures the essential heterojunction electronic structure. The

supporting Au(111) substrate of the experiment (which is not included in the simulation) is expected to

screen long-range built-in fields and may modify precise band-edge energy positions through charge

transfer, hybridization, and image-charge screening. Overall, however, the band-edge energy alignment

observed both in experiment and theory for this metal-semiconductor heterojunction is consistent with a

small energy barrier for hole injection. This implies that GNR-based devices incorporating bottom-up intra-

ribbon contacts as shown here could achieve substantially reduced contact resistance for p-type operation

compared to previous top-down GNR contacting architectures that have so far resulted in extremely poor

contacts.13,18,24,32,54,55

## Conclusion

We have demonstrated the synthesis of a new type of GNR that can be locally switched from a

semiconducting state to a metallic state that is well-described by a quasi-1D zigzag ladder Hamiltonian.

The metallic state is unusual in that it is characterized by two broadly dispersive bands that cross EF, making

it a candidate two-channel conductor. Our ability to write atomically-precise metal-semiconductor

heterojunctions into single GNRs presents new opportunities for low-barrier p-type contacts and future all-

carbon nanoelectronic device architectures.

## Methods

Precursor Synthesis. Full details of the synthesis and characterization of molecular precursor 1 are given

in the Supplementary Information.

Sample Preparation. Atomically-clean Au(111) substrates were prepared using alternating Ar+ sputtering

and annealing cycles under UHV conditions. Sub-monolayer coverages of monomer 1 were prepared via

UHV deposition using a homebuilt Knudsen cell evaporator at a crucible temperature of 130 °C for 10 min

with the substrate held at 24 °C. Polymerization of 1 was achieved by ramping the substrate temperature

by ~5 °C min–1 to T = 180 °C and holding this temperature for 20 min. Cyclodehydrogenation was induced

by ramping the substrate temperature by ~15 °C min–1 to T = 300 °C and holding this temperature for 20

min.

STM Measurements. The molecule-decorated substrate was characterized at each stage of growth using a

commercial Createc low-temperature STM operated at T = 4.7 K with a chemically etched tungsten tip.

STS measurements were conducted using a lock-in amplifier with a modulation frequency f = 533 Hz and

a modulation voltage amplitude of Vac = 4 mV. dI/dV maps were recorded in constant-height mode with

CO-functionalized tips and a modulation voltage amplitude of Vac = 30 mV. BRSTM images were obtained

by mapping the dI/dV signal at zero-bias and constant-height using a CO-functionalized tip. The parameters

for STS peaks were determined by fitting them with Lorentzian line shapes. The average properties for each

feature were extracted from ~20 spectra obtained from six different GNRs using different STM tips. STM

images were processed using the WSxM software56 package.

STM Tip Manipulation. Tip-induced dehydrogenation was performed by placing the STM tip above the

site of a 5-membered ring at an initial tunnel current of 10–200 pA and VS = ±0.2 V. The current feedback

loop was then disabled and the sample voltage was ramped from 0 to ±2.5 V and then back to 0 V while

recording the tunnel current.


<!-- Page 14 -->


14

Calculations. First-principles DFT-LDA calculations were performed using the Quantum ESPRESSO

package.57,58 Norm-conserving (NC) pseudopotentials were employed59,60 with an energy cutoff of 90 Ry

and Gaussian smearing of 0.002 Ry. A vacuum layer of 10 Å was applied along all non-periodic directions

to ensure the accuracy of the results. Chemical structures were fully relaxed until the forces on all atoms

were smaller than 0.01 eV Å–1. Band structure calculations were performed using 40 k-points along the

periodic direction. The Wannier90 package61 was used for performing Wannierization from DFT-LDA

results, and the PythTB package62 was used to obtain tight-binding parameters.

# Quantum Theory of Exciton Magnetic Moment: Interaction and Quantum

# Geometric Effects

Authors: Gurjyot Sethi1,2, Jiawei Ruan1,2, Fang Zhang1,2, Weichen Tang1,2, Chen Hu1,2, Mit Naik1,2, and

Steven G. Louie1,2*

Affiliations:

1Department of Physics, University of California at Berkeley, Berkeley, CA, USA.

2Materials Sciences Division, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, CA, USA.

*Corresponding author: sglouie@berkeley.edu (S.G.L.)

Abstract Combining magnetometry with optical spectroscopy has uncovered novel quantum phenomena and is emerging as a powerful probe of quantum materials. However, the theory of the magnetic response of excitons, correlated electron-hole pairs in insulators, remains incomplete due to insufficient treatment of electron-hole interactions and quantum geometric effects. In biased bilayer graphene, for instance, theoretical predictions of valley g-factors for p-excitons deviate from experiment by nearly an order of magnitude. Here, we develop a quantum theory of the exciton orbital magnetic moment, based on first-order perturbation theory within the GW plus Bethe-Salpeter Equation approach and a rigorous treatment of the position operator in the response of exciton states to a magnetic field. Our formalism reveals three distinct contributions that go beyond the heuristic approaches used in the literature: a Berry-phase-corrected single-particle electron and hole moment difference, a term from envelope-function winding linked to electron-hole relative motion, and a center-ofmass correction from exciton band quantum geometry, with the latter two being completely new effects not considered in previous studies. Our ab initio calculations yield results in excellent agreement with experiment, establishing the importance of interaction and quantum geometric effects in the magnetic response of excitons. Using light to probe quantum materials has elucidated a wide range of phenomena, from energy gaps (1) and excitonic resonances (2) to collective excitations (3). More recently, combining optics with magnetometry has emerged as a powerful probe of correlated and topological matter, with the magnetic response of optical excitations providing access to magnetic order (4), optical control of magnetism (5, 6), and underlying quantum geometry (7, 8). Central to these phenomena are excitons, correlated electron-hole (e-h) pairs that dominate the optical response of gapped systems, particularly in low-dimensional materials (9). The response of excitons to external magnetic fields in two-dimensional (2D) semiconductors has attracted significant attention, in particular, due to its relevance to valleytronics. For example, in 2D systems with three-fold rotational symmetry and broken inversion symmetry, such as transition metal dichalcogenides (10-13) and biased multilayer graphene (14), valley degrees of freedom couple to external magnetic fields via Berry curvature (7, 15, 16), giving rise to measurable Zeeman splitting of excitonic resonances, commonly quantified by an effective exciton valley g-factor. Despite extensive experimental progress, a rigorous quantum mechanical theory of the response of excitons to an external magnetic field remains incomplete. To first order, the energy shift of a particle is proportional to its magnetic moment, including both spin and orbital contributions. Conventional approaches approximate the exciton orbital magnetic moment either as the difference of single-particle (band-state) electron and hole contributions (17-19) at a critical k point or as an average of band-state contributions over the Brillouin-zone (BZ) weighted by the k-space exciton envelope function (20). These treatments neglect electron-hole

interactions, internal exciton structure, and center-of-mass (COM) dynamics, and fail in systems such as biased bilayer graphene, where predicted p-exciton g-factors deviate from experiment by nearly an order of magnitude (14). The underlying difficulty lies in the proper and full treatment of the orbital magnetic moment operator which involves the position operator matrix elements in extended Bloch states basis (21-23). These matrix elements contain singular terms proportional to !!"($ −$") and neglecting these leads to incomplete and gauge-dependent results. The issue is further amplified for excitons, which are composite quasiparticles with both internal and COM Bloch-state character. In this work, we develop a quantum mechanical theory of the exciton orbital magnetic moment within the many-body GW plus Bethe-Salpeter equation (GW-BSE) approach (24, 25). By introducing a periodic analogue of the position operator and constructing localized exciton wave packets in the COM coordinate, we resolve the divergences of the position operator in Bloch basis, and obtain, in the appropriate limits, a gaugeinvariant expression for the exciton orbital magnetic moment. A schematic of our approach is shown in Fig. 1a. We show that the exciton orbital magnetic moment naturally decomposes into contributions from Berryphase-corrected single-particle moments, winding of the exciton envelope function, and a previously overlooked term arising from exciton band quantum geometry (Fig. 1b). We compute the exciton valley gfactors for s- and p-type excitons in biased bilayer graphene (BBG), and the results show excellent agreement with experiment, resolving the discrepancies exhibited in prior theories. We next compute the exciton orbital magnetic moment (the full Eqs. 4 and 5) in biased bilayer graphene (BBG), where exciton valley g-factors have been experimentally measured (14). We perform DFT calculations including hBN encapsulation (Fig. 2a), followed by GW (24) and GW-BSE (25) calculations for quasiparticle bands and excitons (see SM Sec. 7 (26)). For an applied field of 0.10 eV/Å, the quasiparticle gap is 161 meV, significantly enhanced over DFT. The bands near K and K′ exhibit a Mexican-hat dispersion (Fig. 2b), with a clear particle-hole asymmetry, leading to a finite difference in single-particle orbital magnetic moments (Fig. 2c) (also see SM Sec. 8 (26)). As seen in previous theoretical (32) and experimental studies (14), the optical absorption spectrum (Fig. 3a) shows two bright excitons below the gap (32), corresponding to s- and p-type excitons at & = 0. Their envelope functions (Fig. 3b, 3c) display distinct phase structures: the s-exciton is node-less, while the p exciton exhibits a 2k phase winding and a node, consistent with angular momentum +1. The following discussion is based on a gauge choice in which the lowest s-exciton envelope function has a uniform phase (38). Since the excitons are degenerate at & = 0, to evaluate the &-covariant derivatives we further choose a basis within the degenerate subspace in which the two exciton envelope functions are localized in opposite valleys. The Berry-phase correction to the single-particle term is substantial, contributing +2.23 (s) and +3.32  (p), and is enhanced for the p-exciton due to its envelope function localization in regions of large electron and hole Berry curvature (see SM Fig. S4 (26)). moments of the underlying conduction and valence band states and is therefore similar for both s- and p-type excitons, apart from the envelope-function averaging. The relative-motion contribution is negligible for the s-exciton but large and negative for the p-exciton (−5.95), reflecting the phase winding of the p-exciton envelope function. The s-exciton has no envelopefunction winding since there is no angular momentum associated with the e-h relative motion. In contrast, for it to be optically active, the phase winding the envelope function of the p-exciton in k-space is constrained by the winding-number optical selection rule (32) to compensate the winding of the inter-band transition dipole matrix elements. Since the latter is determined by the chirality of the underlying conduction and valence Bloch states, the relative-motion contribution necessarily for the optically active p-exciton acquires the opposite sign to the single-particle contribution. The COM contribution shows a similar trend, with a small value for the s-exciton (−1.22) and a larger magnitude for the p-exciton (−4.78). This contribution originates from the quantum geometry of the exciton band structure and the exchange-driven valley pseudospin texture. Within the effective & ∙y description (33), the inter-valley exchange matrix element is proportional to the optical transition dipole moment ⟨0|yF|@KF⟩, whose phase winding follows that of the exciton envelope function. Consequently, the COM pseudospin winding has the same chirality as the envelope-function winding and therefore contributes with the same sign as the relative-motion term discussed above. Because the p-exciton is optically brighter and undergoes much stronger inter-valley exchange mixing, this quantum-geometric contribution is substantially larger than that for the s-exciton. As a result, the two contributions, the relative-motion angular momentum and the COM quantum geometry, both oppose the single-particle contribution, leading to a near cancellation for the p-exciton and hence its very small magnetic moment. In contrast, the s-exciton possesses neither relative-motion angular momentum nor significant exchange-induced COM pseudospin, so its magnetic moment remains dominated by the singleparticle contribution. The strong suppression of the p-exciton g-factor is therefore a direct consequence of the symmetry and chirality of the exciton wavefunction rather than an accidental cancellation. This highlights the essential roles of exciton quantum geometry and envelope-function structure in determining the magnetic response of excitons, effects that are absent in previous theoretical treatments. In summary, we have derived, within the GW-BSE formalism (25), a complete quantum-mechanical expression for the exciton orbital magnetic moment by rigorously treating the position operator in the Bloch basis and incorporating electron-hole interaction and quantum-geometric effects. The resulting gauge-invariant expression naturally separates the exciton magnetic moment into Berry-phase-corrected single-particle, relative-motion, and COM quantum-geometric contributions. Applying this theory to biased bilayer graphene, we obtain exciton valley g-factors in quantitative agreement with experiment, resolving the discrepancy with previous theoretical approaches and revealing the physical origin of the strongly suppressed p-exciton magnetic moment. Our formalism is general for any periodic crystalline materials and is not restricted to valley systems or two-dimensional materials. For three-dimensional crystals, Eq. 4 is directly applicable for magnetic fields applied along any direction. For two-dimensional materials, the present implementation applies to outof-plane magnetic fields. The extension to in-plane magnetic fields is straightforward, which requires a careful treatment of the out-of-plane position operator and will be presented elsewhere. The methodology developed here is also not limited to the particle-hole BSE formalism. The same perturbative framework, based on constructing the magnetic-field-perturbed two-particle Hamiltonian in the unperturbed correlated two-particle state basis together with the periodic treatment of the position operator, can be extended to other two-particle channels, e.g. using a particle-particle BSE formalism (39). Finally, the present framework can be naturally extended to incorporate full-spinor wavefunctions, the full electron-hole interaction kernel beyond the Tamm-Dancoff approximation (25), and systems with degenerate bands, where

This term arises from phase winding of the exciton wavefunction in &-space, while the covariant derivative also involves the exciton-band Berry connection and is linked to the anomalous COM velocity contribution in external fields (31). These terms demonstrate that, despite its charge neutrality, the exciton COM motion contributes nontrivially to its orbital magnetic moment through the exciton-band quantum geometry. Sensitivity of computed exciton g-factor on G0W0 starting point: We note that the exact values of the computed exciton g-factors depend on the underlying quasiparticle electronic structure, since the exciton magnetic moment (Eq. 4) is given in terms of the quasiparticle energy derivatives, inter-band Berry connections, and velocity matrix elements. Different mean-field starting points for G0W0 may therefore lead to some variation in the calculated exciton orbital magnetic moments. However, the low-energy electronic structure of BBG is confined to the carbon-pz manifold (Fig. S1a (26)), whose orbital character is expected to be relatively insensitive to the choice of exchange-correlation functional. Consequently, the dependence on the G0W0 starting point is expected to be weak (See SM Sec. 10 (26)). The physical trends and the origin of the different contributions are, moreover, robust against appreciable changes in the underlying electronic structure. This is seen in the calculations for different BBG/hBN structures (see SM Sec. 7 (26)), which consistently exhibit a dominant single-particle contribution for the s-exciton and strong cancellation between the three contributions for the p-exciton. Thus, the decomposition of the exciton magnetic moment into single-particle, relative-motion, and COM quantum-geometric contributions, together with the physical mechanism responsible for the suppression of the p-exciton magnetic moment, remains unchanged. General convention for exciton wavefunction with finite center-of-mass momentum: We further show in the SM Sec. 9 (26) that the theory can be formulated using a general convention for the exciton wavefunction with an arbitrary momentum-partition parameter (z), i.e., defined using the free e-h pair basis given by |3, $ + (1 −z)&⟩⨂|2, $ −α&⟩∗, instead of the symmetric convention used above (z = 1/2). This allows the theory to be implemented directly using a different momentum convention adopted by different GW-BSE codes without requiring an explicit transformation to the symmetric convention. Methods Ab initio calculations of the electronic structure of BBG were performed using density functional theory (DFT) within the local density approximation (LDA) for the exchange-correlation functional, as implemented in the Quantum ESPRESSO package (7). Optimized norm-conserving Vanderbilt pseudopotentials were employed (8). The Kohn-Sham orbitals were expanded in a plane-wave basis with a kinetic energy cutoff of 70 Ry. To eliminate spurious interactions between periodic images, we applied a truncated Coulomb interaction in the out-of-plane direction (9) and included a vacuum spacing of 20 Å, following extensive convergence tests. Structural relaxation for pristine BBG was carried out until the forces on atoms were below 10:M &r/Å, yielding an inplane lattice constant of u = 2.448 Å (see Fig. S2). To simulate hBN encapsulation, monolayers of hBN were placed above and below BBG, assuming a commensurate in-plane lattice constant. The out-of-plane atomic positions were then relaxed to the same force tolerance as above, yielding interlayer distances of 3.329 Å between carbon layers and 3.216 Å between carbon and hBN layers. Among the various high-symmetry stacking configurations, the most energetically favorable arrangement places boron directly over the carbon sites, while nitrogen avoids direct overlap with carbon atoms in AB-stacked BBG. Depending on whether boron lies above/below A or B sublattices of graphene, there are four possible configurations, one of which is used in Fig. 2a, where boron atoms are placed over the non-dimer sites of BBG. It should be noted that in pristine BBG the valence and conduction band edges are contributed by the non-dimer sites (10). In Fig. S3, we show results for an alternative stacking in which the boron atom sits over a dimer site on one side and a non-dimer site on the other. While DFT-LDA provides reliable Kohn-Sham orbitals as quasiparticle wavefunctions, it underestimates band gaps and band dispersion. To address this issue, we carried out single-shot G0W0 calculations (1) using the BerkeleyGW package (11) to obtain quasiparticle self-energy corrections to the band energies. The static dielectric matrix was computed within the random phase approximation using a plane-wave cutoff of 8 Ry and 1,000 unoccupied bands. To accelerate convergence with respect to BZ sampling, we employed the non-uniform neck subsampling (NNS) technique (12). A 24  ×  24  ×  1 Monkhorst-Pack grid with ten NNS points was used for dielectric function and self-energy calculations. Due to the huge band gap of hBN, the effect of hBN on the dielectric screening of BG is small, hence we assume the dielectric matrix to be the same for pristine BBG and BBG with hBN. The resulting quasiparticle band structure (Fig. 2b) was interpolated using maximally localized Wannier functions generated with the Wannier90 code (13). Excitonic properties were computed by solving the BSE on top of the GW-corrected band structure (14), again using the BerkeleyGW package (11). We used a patched sampling scheme focusing on the K and K′ valleys, achieving an effective resolution equivalent to a 900  ×  900 uniform mesh, which ensured convergence of exciton energies to within 5 meV. The exciton orbital magnetic moment is then evaluated with perturbation theory using the expressions derived in this work. This perturbative treatment, together with the fixed-screening approximation, allows the first-order magnetic response to be expressed entirely in terms of the I-dependent unperturbed exciton energies and wavefunctions. To assess the effect of hBN encapsulation and stacking, we compared excitonic orbital magnetic moments for pristine BBG and both hBN/BBG configurations as described above. hBN encapsulation introduces sublattice symmetry breaking in each graphene layer, enhancing particle– hole asymmetry and increasing the difference between conduction and valence band single-particle orbital magnetic moments. This trend is evident in the comparison between Fig. S2 (pristine) and Fig. 2c (encapsulated), leading to a significant impact on the valley g-factors. Further we compare values for the two hBN/BBG configurations studied – i.e., values in Table 1 vs values in Fig. S3. For the two configurations, the s-exciton g-factors are 13.48 and 20.32, while the p-exciton values are 2.58 and 1.76. In both cases, the disparity between s- and p-exciton magnetic responses persists, and the newly derived contributions dominate the final value of the g-factor for the case of p-exciton. Among the two stacking configurations, the one with boron on the non-dimer carbon sites shows better agreement with experiment. While our simulations do not account for the incommensurability between graphene and hBN lattices, this comparison suggests that such a stacking arrangement may have been prominent in experimental samples. 8. The weak dependence of the computed values of the exciton magnetic moment in BBG on the DFT mean-field starting point for the G0W0 quasiparticle calculation can be understood from its low-energy electronic structure. The bands relevant to the excitons considered here belong to the carbon-pz manifold (Fig. S1a). Their sublattice and layer hybridization is primarily governed by the lattice geometry, interlayer coupling, and applied bias. Changing the exchangecorrelation approximation therefore only slightly renormalizes the DFT parameters within the same low-energy manifold rather than changing its orbital character or qualitatively reconstructing the corresponding wavefunctions. Since at the G0W0 level the mean-field DFT energies and wavefunctions are used as approximations to the quasiparticle quantities in the construction of the self-energy operator, we consequently expect the quantities entering the exciton magnetic moment to be relatively insensitive to the exchange-correlation functional used. We explicitly verify this by calculating the DFT single-particle orbital magnetic moments of the relevant valence and conduction bands using LDA, PBE, and SCAN. As shown in Fig. S5, the difference between the conduction and valence-band orbital moments, which directly enters the single-particle contribution to the exciton magnetic moment, exhibits very little variation among the three functionals. The individual band moments likewise show only weak dependence on the exchange-correlation approximation. We have also performed G0W0 calculations starting from each of the three functionals. As shown in Fig. S6, the resulting quasiparticle band dispersions remain very similar, with the quasiparticle band gap varying by only a few meV among the three starting points. Thus, both the wavefunction-dependent quantum geometric quantities and the quasiparticle energies and band dispersion relevant to our full exciton magnetic-moment calculation are only very weakly affected by the choice among these starting points. Finally, the exciton envelope functions are obtained from the Bethe-Salpeter equation, whose matrix elements depend on the underlying single-particle wavefunctions, screened electronhole interaction, and quasiparticle dispersions. Given the very similar low-energy wavefunctions and quasiparticle band structures obtained from the three starting points, we expect the resulting exciton wavefunctions, and hence the calculated exciton valley g-factors, to exhibit correspondingly weak dependence on the choice of starting point. 11. ## Abstract:

Kagome lattices provide a simple geometry for engineering electronic states that exhibit novel quantum behavior. In conventional kagome materials, however, the relevant states are often embedded in chemically complex three-dimensional crystals and are difficult to isolate or tune. Molecule-based kagome networks offer structural precision and tunability, but have largely been confined to metallic substrates incompatible with 2D devices. Here we report growth of singlelayer Ni3(HITP)2 metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) on van der Waals substrates including graphene-based field-effect devices using metal-salt molecular beam epitaxy. Low-temperature scanning tunneling spectroscopy resolves kagome-derived flat-band and van Hove singularitybased spectral features consistent with first-principles calculations. Gating hybrid 2D MOF devices allows us to energetically shift kagome spectral features, thus establishing electrostatic control of chemically programmable 2D kagome electronic lattices.


<!-- Page 2 -->


2

Main

2D kagome lattices provide a route to achieve flat electronic bands, Dirac crossings, van Hove singularities, and the novel correlated and topological physics associated with these band structure features.1-3 A central challenge, however, is the realization of 2D kagome systems that are structurally well-defined and have a continuously tunable Fermi energy (EF), since this is not yet achievable using conventional solid-state kagome materials.3-6 Bulk kagome metals such as AV3Sb5 and RMn6Sn6 exhibit novel superconductivity, charge order, and topological magnetism,7-

10 but their electronic structures typically deviate significantly from ideal 2D kagome characteristics and they are not easily integrated with 2D gate-tunable device platforms.3,4,11,12 Molecular kagome networks offer an alternate route for accessing kagome-based physics because their lattice geometry and orbital structure can be flexibly programmed through chemical synthesis. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), for example, allow atomically-precise 2D kagome lattices to be engineered from organic linkers and metal coordination nodes.13-18 Up to now, however, kagome MOFs have mainly been grown on bulk metal substrates that are incompatible with device-based electronic tunability.19-22

We have overcome this limitation by growing single-layer kagome MOFs directly on semiconducting and semimetal bulk van der Waals (vdW) substrates, as well as on monolayer (ML) graphene/hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) field-effect (FET) devices. Combined scanning tunneling microscopy (STM), scanning tunneling spectroscopy (STS), and first principles electronic structure calculations show that our bottom-up fabricated MOFs exhibit expected 2D kagome electronic structure features. Our MOF growth was accomplished using a novel metal-salt molecular beam epitaxy (metal-salt MBE) approach to obtain well-ordered covalently-bonded kagome domains at the surface of graphite and WSe2 bulk crystals as well as ML-graphene/hBN devices. Here the transition metal component of our MOF is deposited using low-temperature metal bromide evaporation rather than more conventional high-temperature elemental e-beam evaporation.20,23 STM spectroscopy of single-layer kagome MOFs grown at the surfaces of graphite and ML-graphene/hBN show signatures of all the major features expected of a kagome system, including flat bands, van Hove singularities, and Dirac points. These features compare well to ab initio DFT simulations of the electronic structure of isolated single-layer kagome MOFs having identical chemical structure. MOFs grown on ML-graphene/hBN devices have an energy gap of ~ 0.7 eV and exhibit a valence flat band that appears only 0.2 eV below the graphene Dirac point. Electrostatic gating of these devices causes the kagome band structure features to rigidly shift in energy by ±0.12 eV, comparable to the energy shift of bare graphene FET electronic features under identical gating conditions.24,25 These results establish a new device-integrated, chemically programmable 2D molecular kagome platform in which local electronic structure can be imaged and electrostatically tuned.

Design of a single-layer molecular kagome lattice

To realize a chemically-defined kagome lattice compatible with on-surface synthesis and STM imaging in 2D devices, we selected the previously reported MOF Ni3(HITP)2 (HITP = 2,3,6,7,10,11-hexaiminotriphenylene).26 Here square-planar NiN4 coordination nodes are linked by extended -conjugated HITP ligands to form a 2D kagome network of corner-sharing triangles (Fig. 1A). Density functional theory (DFT) simulations of a freestanding Ni3(HITP)2 monolayer (Fig. 1B) reveal a three-band conduction manifold that captures the hallmarks of a kagome lattice: a flat band (FB1) with nearby Dirac point (DP) and flanking van Hove singularities (VHS1 and VHS2). Wannier analysis maps this conduction manifold onto three symmetry-related orbitals centered on the three NiN4 kagome sites that are connected by nearest neighbor and next nearestneighbor hopping (Supplementary Materials Fig. S1). Valence band states are separated from the conduction bands by an energy gap and show a slightly distorted kagome manifold. Here a flat band (FB2) lies below the charge neutrality point and above a van Hove singularity (VHS3). The more complex valence-band dispersion is consistent with stronger mixing between Ni d orbitals and HITP-derived states. At even lower energy a second valence manifold can be seen that exhibits a third flat band (FB3).

Metal-salt molecular beam epitaxy of Ni3(HITP)2 on van der Waals substrates

We first attempted to grow Ni3(HITP)2 on highly oriented pyrolytic graphite (HOPG) using the conventional method of co-depositing elemental Ni and 2,3,6,7,10,11-hexaaminotriphenylene (HATP) molecules (see Supplementary Materials and Methods).20,23 However, this resulted in problematical Ni clustering and disordered molecular adsorption, with no extended kagome lattice formation. We then turned to a new metal-salt MBE growth scheme in which anhydrous NiBr2 and HATP precursors are supplied from separate source crucibles and reacted directly on the growth substrate which is held at elevated temperature (T ≈ 250 °C) to form Ni3(HITP)2 (Fig. 1C). This was motivated by the idea that NiBr2 might suppress metallic Ni aggregation by delivering Ni in a halide-coordinated ionic form that can react with HATP during MOF nucleation.

This new growth scheme resulted in well-ordered single-layer Ni3(HITP)2 kagome lattice domains on HOPG separated by grain boundaries (Fig. 2A, white dashed lines). Higher resolution STM topographs (Fig. 2B) show the kagome lattice constant to be ~19 Å, consistent with the structural model of Fig. 1A. We identify two common defect types: excess HITP molecules residing in lattice pores (red dashed circle) and HITP vacancies (yellow dashed circle), with an overall defect density of ~1012 cm–2. Fourier transforms of our STM images yield sixfoldsymmetric Bragg peaks (Supplementary Materials Fig. S2), consistent with long-range kagome order.27,28

Single-layer kagome lattice growth was also achieved for bulk p-doped WSe2 substrates (Fig. 2, C and D), demonstrating that metal-salt MBE is compatible with different vdW materials. The growth morphology differs, however, depending on the substrate. On HOPG Ni3(HITP)2

forms large islands that merge (Fig. 2A), whereas on WSe2 Ni3(HITP)2 grows in the form of numerous smaller islands that have dendritic character (Fig. 2C). This difference is consistent with the existence of a higher density of growth nucleation sites on WSe2 due to dopants and surface defects that do not occur for graphite (Supplementary Materials Fig. S4).

Local spectroscopic resolution of kagome-derived electronic states

We next tested whether predicted kagome electronic structure can be resolved directly by local STS of Ni3(HITP)2 grown on HOPG. Fig. 3A shows a representative dI/dV spectrum acquired in the interior of a Ni3(HITP)2 domain (STS spectra were acquired at least 10 nm from edges to avoid possible edge effects). The spectrum exhibits pronounced features for filled and empty states that are separated by an energy gap of ΔE ≈ 0.7 eV. On the conduction band side, a prominent peak is seen at Vs ≈ +0.9 V (feature 1) that lies above an “M-shaped” structure with two shoulders (features 2 and 4) flanking a central dip (feature 3). On the valence band side the topmost feature is a strong peak at Vs ≈ – 0.2 V (feature 5), below which several smaller resonances/shoulders lie within a few tens of mV. We label the most prominent of these feature 6. As Vs is reduced the dI/dV signal dips to a minimum at Vs ≈ –0.5 V but then rises to form a prominent resonance centered at Vs ≈ –0.8 V (feature 7).

We spatially resolved the MOF kagome states by recording constant-height dI/dV maps at the energies of the most prominent spectral peaks (i.e., features 1 and 5). As shown in Fig. 3B, the dI/dV map of feature 1 (Vs = +0.9 V) in the conduction band is distributed broadly across the entire MOF framework, including substantial weight on the triphenylene ligands. In contrast, the state corresponding to feature 5 (Vs = –0.2 V) in the valence band is concentrated primarily on the NiN4 nodes with very weak intensity on the organic linkers (Fig. 3C).

To understand the origin of these experimental STS features we calculated the total density of states (DOS) of a freestanding Ni3(HITP)2 monolayer (Fig. 3F). The simulated kagome DOS reproduces the main features of our data quite nicely. In the conduction band, for example, a flatband peak (FB1) is seen that corresponds to experimental feature 1, while a pair of smaller peaks (VHS1 and VHS2) arising from van Hove singularities correspond to experimental features 2 and 4, and a theoretical Dirac point dip (DP) corresponds to experimental feature 3. The overall energy width of the theoretical conduction band features (~0.4 eV) reasonably matches the experimental width (~0.5 eV). On the valence band side the theoretical flat-band peak marked FB2 corresponds well to experimental feature 5. Just below FB2 the match is not as good, but there is a rough correspondence between the theoretical van Hove singularity (VHS3) and experimental feature 6. Below VHS3 both theory and experiment show a significant reduction in spectral density before rising in a strong resonance that shows agreement between theoretical FB3 and experimental feature 7. The general good agreement between theory and experiment extends to the spatial distribution of the kagome electronic states, as seen by comparison of the theoretical LDOS for flat band FB1 (Fig. 3D) and flat band FB2 (Fig. 3E) to the experimental dI/dV images of Fig. 3B


<!-- Page 5 -->


5

and C. Here the filled-state LDOS concentrates primarily on the NiN4 centers whereas the emptystate LDOS extends across the organic ligand for both theory and experiment, including a prominent node at the ligand center.

While there is good agreement between theory and experiment for the main spectroscopic features of Ni3(HITP)2, there remain some discrepancies. For example, the experimental spectral density “tail” below feature 4 is much shorter than the tail seen below the simulated peak of VHS2. This highlights the difficulty in some STM experiments of determining precise band edges when bands exhibit energetically long tails, since the STM tip must be brought very close to the surface to capture small, evanescent features.29,30 In these cases it is difficult to determine the “true” bandgap using STS, and so "functional" energy gaps are often defined instead.31 For the kagome system studied here we define the functional energy gap as the separation between the highest points of the LDOS peaks nearest the valence and conduction band edges, since these features are robust and experimentally unambiguous. Following this protocol allows us to define an experimental energy gap between features 4 and 5 of 0.7 ± 0.1 eV, which we can then compare to the theoretical energy gap between peaks VHS2 and FB2 of 0.45 eV. The smaller calculated gap may partly reflect the well-known tendency of DFT–PBE to underestimate semiconductor bandgaps.32-36 Although these peak separations also depend on the dispersions near the band edges, the overall correspondence between experiment and theory supports this interpretation.

Device integration and electrostatic tuning of kagome-derived states

Our new ability to grow high-quality MOFs on HOPG and semiconducting TMD surfaces opens the possibility of growing 2D kagome lattices directly on single-layer FET devices made from these substrate materials. Our motivation for doing this is that the gate-tunability of such devices provides a possible strategy for tuning the MOF Fermi energy (EF) into interesting regions of the kagome band structure without having to introduce impurity dopants. In order to test the feasibility of this strategy we grew single-layer kagome MOFs on ML-graphene/hBN FET device substrates. The graphene device stacks (Fig. 4A) were assembled using a PVC-based dry pickup technique where graphene and hBN flakes are sequentially stacked and then transferred onto a SiO2/Si substrate, with Si serving as a global back-gate. Cr/Au electrical contacts were then deposited by shadow-mask evaporation to reduce surface contamination (Fig. 4B), and then wirebonded. Graphene devices were AFM-scratched for cleanliness37,38 before putting them into the UHV chamber and annealing at 400 C for 12 hours for additional cleanliness. Device surfaces were checked via STM in UHV to ensure atomic cleanliness (Fig. 4C) before initiating MOF growth in a connected chamber.

Single-layer Ni3(HITP)2 MOFs were grown directly on ML-graphene/hBN devices using the same NiBr2/HATP metal-salt MBE strategy used for HOPG substrates, but with a higher substrate temperature of 320 C compared to 250 C for HOPG. The need for higher temperature here for good growth possibly reflects the lower thermal conductivity of the device stack relative


<!-- Page 6 -->


6

to bulk HOPG or WSe2. STM imaging after performing this growth protocol revealed well-ordered Ni3(HITP)2 kagome domains on the graphene device that are structurally indistinguishable from those obtained on HOPG except for the presence of a large-scale background graphene/hBN moiré pattern (Fig. 4D).

To assess substrate effects in the device geometry we calculated the electronic structure of Ni3(HITP)2 supported on monolayer graphene (Supplementary Materials Fig. S2). The MOFprojected bands retain the characteristic kagome manifolds of the freestanding monolayer, indicating weak hybridization with graphene over the relevant energy range. The Fermi level remains within the MOF-projected gap, with no evidence of appreciable graphene-induced carrier doping in the modeled neutral heterostructure. These results support using the freestanding MOF monolayer calculation to interpret the principal features of MOF/graphene device STS.

We used the Si back-gate of our Ni3(HITP)2/graphene/hBN device to electrostatically tune the electronic structure of a single-layer bottom-up-fabricated kagome lattice. Fig. 5A shows a cartoon sketch of how gating is expected to alter the electronic structure of Ni3(HITP)2/graphene assuming a simple “rigid band” model where increased gate-voltage (VG) causes an increase in EF. Fig. 5B shows a density map of the STM dI/dV signal measured as a function of Vs and VG with the STM tip held at a single point above the kagome overlayer. The vertical blue band bracketing Vs = 0 shows the same experimental kagome energy gap seen in Fig. 3A. To the left of this is a vertical red feature that arises from the high DOS of kagome feature 5 in the filled states (i.e., flat band 2 (FB2)). This feature has a negative slope with Vs, indicating that FB2 shifts down in energy as VG is increased (consistent with rigid band motion as sketched in Fig. 5A). Other kagome electronic structure features, such as feature 1 in the empty states (FB1) and feature 7 at lower Vs (FB3) similarly shift down in energy with increased VG at a rate of ∂E/∂VG ≈ –3 meV/V, thus demonstrating the overall gate-tunability of single-layer kagome electronic structure (See Supplementary Materials Fig. S5 for detailed FB peak shift analysis).

Closer inspection of Fig. 5B reveals a set of sharp resonances that move with positive slope as Vs is increased (green arrows). We attribute these features to charging events involving localized states, most likely associated with defects that trap charge in or near the Ni3(HITP)2 layer.39,40 These resonances are different from the “normal” DOS features discussed above and behave similar to quantum dot charging behavior observed previously that is characterized by “Coulomb diamonds” as Vs and VG are varied.41,42 In some cases we observe these charging features to be accompanied by abrupt local shifts of nearby kagome-derived spectral features (yellow arrows), consistent with local charge-induced modification of the electrostatic environment near the STM tip.


<!-- Page 7 -->


7

Conclusion and outlook

We have demonstrated a new strategy for achieving single-layer MOF kagome lattices whose local electronic structure can be imaged and electrostatically tuned in a van der Waals device geometry. Metal-salt MBE enables MOF growth on weakly interacting substrates, avoiding the bulk metal substrates that have historically limited device control of on-surface-synthesized molecular networks. Low-temperature STS resolves kagome-derived spectral features, including narrow flat-band peaks and van Hove singularity features, consistent with first-principles calculations. Integration of metal-salt MBE growth of MOFs with ML-graphene/hBN FET devices enables observation of gate-dependent energy shifts of the kagome spectral density. Future improved devices should allow stronger gating that enables the device EF to be shifted directly into interesting regions of the 2D kagome band structure, such as flat bands, Dirac points, and van Hove singularities.

## Abstract

Topological design of -electrons in zigzag-edged graphene nanoribbons (ZGNRs) leads

to a wealth of magnetic quantum phenomena and exotic quantum phases.1-9 Symmetric

ZGNRs typically exhibit antiferromagnetically coupled spin-ordered edge states.1,2

Eliminating cross-edge magnetic coupling in ZGNRs not only enables the realization of

a new class of ferromagnetic quantum spin chains,10 enabling the exploration of

quantum spin physics and entanglement of multiple qubits in the 1D limit,3,11 but also

establishes a long-sought carbon-based ferromagnetic transport channel, pivotal for

ultimate scaling of GNR-based quantum electronics.1-3,9,12 Here, we report a general

approach for designing and fabricating such ferromagnetic GNRs in the form of Janus

GNRs (JGNRs) with two distinct edge configurations. Guided by Lieb's theorem and

topological classification theory,13-15 we devised two JGNRs by asymmetrically

introducing a topological defect array of benzene motifs to one zigzag edge, while

keeping the opposing zigzag edge unchanged. This breaks structural symmetry and

creates a sublattice imbalance within each unit cell, initiating a spin symmetry breaking.

Three 'Z-shape' precursors are designed to fabricate one parent ZGNR and two JGNRs

with an optimal lattice spacing of the defect array for a complete quench of the

magnetic edge states at the “defective” edge. Characterization via scanning probe

microscopy/spectroscopy and first-principles density functional theory confirms the

successful fabrication of JGNRs with ferromagnetic ground state delocalised along the

pristine zigzag edge.

## Introduction

The term "Janus" has been adopted to denote materials that exhibit different properties on

two opposing sides or faces.16,17 In the realm of 2D materials, creating asymmetric Janus

materials by breaking the top- and bottom-layer symmetry, provides an attractive route for

engineering novel properties and functionalities such as enhanced valley spin splitting, out-

of-plane piezoelectricity and second harmonic generation.18-21 Reducing the dimension of

Janus materials from 2D to 1D systems with two different edge structures/topologies (hence

properties), especially those with asymmetric zigzag edge in JGNRs, creates new

opportunities for the realization of 1D ferromagnetic quantum spin chains and the assembly

of multiple qubits. It also enables the creation of ferromagnetic transport channel in the 1D

limit,22,23 which can carry completely spin polarized current without applying in-plane

electric field,24 strain25 or chemical functionalizations,26,27 as required for conventional

ZGNRs. These features are crucial for advancing the miniaturization of spintronic devices

with enhanced energy efficiency.28

Although theoretical attempts have been made to break the zigzag structural symmetry by

attaching triangular fragments to one zigzag edge of the ZGNR, the resulting ferromagnetic

state is more delocalized and extends into the triangular fragments.29 Moreover, the

experimental exploration of such GNRs remain elusive, as the rational design of precursors

towards such novel GNRs requires the simultaneous breaking of their structural and spin

symmetries. This task is even more challenging than fabricating symmetric ZGNRs, which is

notoriously difficult due to the high reactivity of zigzag edges combined with the challenges

in intricate design and synthesis of precursors. To date, only two symmetric ZGNRs have

been reported, both based on the 'U-shape' precursor design. Moreover, the width of the

obtained ZGNRs is limited to having six carbon zigzag chains across the ribbon, namely, 6-

ZGNR.1,2

The design principle for JGNRs

Our strategy for creating such JGNRs involves decorating one zigzag edge of ZGNRs with a

topological “defect” array (termed as TDZ edge), while keeping the other zigzag edge

unchanged. Guided by this principle, we introduce a periodic array of benzene motifs


<!-- Page 4 -->


attached to the TDZ edge to break structural symmetry and to create a sublattice imbalance

within each unit cell (∆𝑁 = 1), leaving one unpaired electron in each unit cell (Fig. 2).13,30 As

a result, this introduces a zero-energy band in line with Lieb's theorem, initiating the spin

symmetry breaking in this system.31-33 To effectively quench the spin at the TDZ edge and

maintain a single ferromagnetic edge-state band at the zigzag edge, the key is to determine

the optimal spacing (denoted as m, m=1, 2, 3, etc) between periodic benzene rings at the TDZ

edge, which can maximally disrupts the edge states. To achieve this, we applied the

topological classification using chiral symmetry developed in Ref. 15. In 1D bipartite lattices

such as GNRs, because of the negligible second-nearest-neighbour interactions, chiral

symmetry is satisfied, leading to a Z-classification of electronic topological phases with a

conventional 𝑍 index.15 As the 𝑍 index is 0 for vacuum (which is a topological trivial phase),

the count of end states can be deduced from the 𝑍 index of the GNRs.

For our design principle, we employ an important correspondence here that the edge of a

JGNR (which can be either a defective zigzag edge or a normal zigzag edge) can be viewed

as the end of a wide armchair-edged GNR (AGNR) in the large width limit (Fig. S1). This

means the existence and characteristics of the topological edge states of a defective zigzag

edge are similar to the topological end states of a large-width AGNR with a similar defective

structure at its end. When examining the topological behavior of the end of an AGNR, the 𝑍

index can be expressed in a straightforward form15:
