Since (m = 2)-JGNR is predicted to feature the unique ferromagnetic ground state with a

single ferromagnetic zigzag edge, our study focuses on the synthesis and investigation of this

type of JGNRs. Here, we used the notation (n,m)-JGNRs to describe the specific JGNRs,

where n refers to the number of carbon zigzag chain laterally across the ribbon and m denotes

the benzene ring spacing at the TDZ edge, as defined above. Specifically, we target to

fabricate the (4,2)- and (5,2)-JGNRs (Fig. 2) with different width and the parent 5-ZGNR

(Fig.3) (which can also be viewed as the corresponding (5,∞)-JGNR) to experimentally

validate our topological theory predictions and our design principle.

Precursor design for on-surface synthesis of JGNRs

To achieve the on-surface synthesis of two JGNRs (with n = 4 and 5, m = 2), we employ a Z-

shaped molecular precursor design for the asymmetric fabrication, in contrast with the U-

shaped precursor used previously for the on-surface synthesis of the 6-ZGNR.34-37 The Z-

shaped precursor comprises of two independent branch moieties that are interconnected by a

single C-C bond. At the termini of the branches, two bromine atoms are strategically

positioned as connection sites for thermally induced aryl-aryl coupling. The Z-shaped

precursor design also allows for the independent modification of individual branches,

facilitating a separate control over the two edge geometries of the resulting JGNRs. Utilizing

methylphenanthrene groups for both branches (precursor 3 in Fig. 3) yields two identical

zigzag edges, corresponding to the conventional 5-ZGNR. Intriguingly, substituting one of

the methylphenanthrene groups to an oligophenyl group results in the modification of one of

the zigzag edges to our target TDZ edge with periodically decorated benzene rings (with a

spacing of m = 2). Additionally, adjusting the length of the oligophenyl groups from biphenyl

to triphenyl (precursor 1 and 2 in Fig. 2) enables the modulation of the width of the JGNRs

from n=4 to n=5.

The precursors were successfully obtained via multi-step organic synthesis (see

Supplementary Information) and then separately deposited onto a clean Au(111) surface

under ultrahigh vacuum (UHV) using a Knudsen cell evaporator. Stepwise annealing of the

precursor decorated surfaces induces polymerization and cyclodehydrogenation reactions to


<!-- Page 7 -->


yield the corresponding (4,2)- and (5,2)-JGNRs (Fig. 2) and 5-ZGNR (Fig. 3). The yield of

all the GNRs is low under our experimental conditions (Fig. S12 and S13), primarily due to

the flexible backbone of the corresponding polymers, which undergo random

cyclodehydrogenation reactions during thermal annealing (Fig. S11). In addition, the

asymmetric precursors 1 and 2 offer limited control over different polymerization modes

(Fig. S14), namely head-to-tail, and head-to-head (or termed as tail-to-tail). If polymerization

proceeds in a head-to-head (tail-to-tail) configuration, then the resulting GNRs will feature

alternative cove and gulf regions on both edges.35,36 Here, we focus on the investigation of

the targeted JGNRs through the head-to-tail polymerization. The topographic STM images of

both (4,2)-JGNR and (5,2)-JGNR reveal a characteristic height profile and morphology

featuring bright lobes at the intact zigzag edge and larger protrusions at the TDZ edge,

corresponding to the position of periodically-spaced benzene rings. The bond-resolved

scanning tunnelling microscopy (BR-STM) images of both JGNRs acquired at -10 mV using

a CO-functionalized tip exhibit the corrugated hexagon-like rings in the centre and distorted

lobe features along the edges, which are presumably attributed to the perturbations induced

by the electronic states of the JGNRs in the vicinity of Fermi level (EF).38,39 In contrast, the

BR-STM image of 5-ZGNR acquired at 10 mV using a CO-functionalized tip clearly resolves

the characteristic hexagon patterns in the backbone, indicating an absence of electronic states

near EF.

To better resolve the backbone framework of both JGNRs, we further conducted the qPlus

sensor-based non-contact atomic force microscopy (nc-AFM) images, which relies on

monitoring the resonance frequency shift of an oscillating quartz force sensor as the CO

functionalized tip scans over the sample in the Pauli repulsive regime.40,41 The achieved

resolution directly confirms the different edge morphologies correspond to the expected

JGNRs as defined by the precursor design. It is noted that the outer benzene rings on the TDZ

edge appear flattened along the ribbon and larger in size than the ones in the backbone, while

the outer rings at the intact zigzag edges appear stretched in the direction perpendicular to the

ribbon. Such a different appearance of hexagons at different edges of JGNRs is presumably

due to varying degrees of CO-tip bending effect due to different edge topologies.  All these

results prove the success of the Z-shape precursor design strategy for the synthesis of both

JGNRs and 5-ZGNR.

Scanning tunnelling spectroscopy of the GNRs.

Previous studies revealed magnetic edge states cannot be directly observed in the wider 6-

ZGNR and N-doped 6-ZGNR when sitting on Au(111), because they coupled strongly to the

metal substrate.1,2 Compared to 6-ZGNR, both 5-ZGNR and two JGNRs have a narrow

ribbon width, thus leading to a more rigid backbone that could prevent a strong structural

downward bending and electronic coupling with substrate.42 Our differential conductance

(dI/dV) spectroscopic measurements acquired over both 5-ZGNR and JGNRs combined with

theoretical calculations confirm that magnetic edge states can survive on Au(111) for these

narrower ribbons (Fig. 3).  dI/dV spectrum obtained at the edge of 5-ZGNR show three

distinct peaks located at 760 ± 18 mV (peak A), -300 ± 5 mV (peak B), and -410 ± 7 mV

(peak C), yielding an apparent experimental band gap of  ∆𝐸𝑒𝑥𝑝= 1060 ± 19 meV (Fig. 3c

and Fig. S5). Our experimental gap of 5-ZGNR is smaller than that of the 6-ZGNR (1.5 eV)

placed on top of a monolayer NaCl island.1 Such behaviour is likely attributed to the

screening effect of the metal substrate in reducing the quasiparticle energies and band gaps of

reduced dimensional systems.43-46 The dI/dV maps recorded at the biases corresponding to

these three peak energies reveal the characteristic lobe features predominately located at both

zigzag edges, demonstrating reproducible patterns in the DFT-calculated local density of

states (LDOS) maps of each of the frontier band states (Figure 3d-f). Note that the slight

asymmetry in the dI/dV maps of the edge states is presumably arose from tip asymmetry.

As shown in Fig. 4a, dI/dV spectrum taken over the zigzag edge of (4,2)-JGNR also reveals

three noticeable features located at 581 ± 19 mV (peak A), 45 ± 5 mV (peak B) and -487 ± 14

mV (peak C), which yields an apparent band gap of  ∆𝐸𝑒𝑥𝑝= 536 ± 9 meV for (4,2)-JGNR.

However, peak C is absent in the dI/dV curve taken over the additional benzene ring of the

TDZ edge. The most pronounced peak B spans across EF, which is tentatively assigned as the

partially-filled top VB (spin down and localized mainly along the intact zigzag edge) arising

from the charge transfer due to the work function difference between GNR and Au(111).

dI/dV image (Fig. 4c) acquired at the energy positions of peak B shows a petal-shaped feature

on the zigzag edge and flower-shaped features distributed on the entire backbone of the (4,2)-

JGNR. In contrast, the spatial distribution of other two peaks of the (4,2)-JGNRs reveal

similar characteristic zigzag lobe features predominately or exclusively located at the intact

zigzag edges for peak A and peak C, respectively (Fig. 4b, 4d, and Fig. S18). Similarly (Fig.

4j), dI/dV spectrum of (5,2)-JGNR also reveals three peak structures centered at 410 ± 11 mV


<!-- Page 9 -->


(peak A), 16 ± 2 mV (peak B) and -510 ± 14 mV (peak C), which yields a smaller apparent

band gap of ∆𝐸𝑒𝑥𝑝= 394 ± 9 meV. Compared to (4,2)-JGNR, all the states observed in

(5,2)-JGNR experience a slight downward shift in energy, but their spatial distribution

patterns in the dI/dV maps are rather similar (Fig. 4k-4m, and Fig. S19).

Ab initio calculation of JGNRs electronic structures

A direct capture of spectroscopic features and their wave function patterns of electronic states

for both 5-ZGNRs and two JGNRs suggest a relatively weak coupling of the ribbons with the

Au(111) substrate. We thus conducted ab initio density functional theory (DFT) calculations

within the local spin density approximation (LSDA) to calculate spin-polarized electronic

structures for the free-standing ZGNRs and JGNRs.  Our first-principles results offer

quantitative evidence that the 5-ZGNR and two JGNRs synthesized on Au(111) all maintain

their intrinsic magnetic edge states. Panels in Fig. 3g-3i present the calculated LDOS maps

acquired at the energies corresponding to peak A' (conduction band minimum), peak B'

(valence band maximum), and peak C' (the valence band states near the Brillouin zone edge

X) of the freestanding 5-ZGNR, respectively. The distinctive pattern and relative contrast of

protrusions lining the edges of 5-ZGNRs observed in experimental dI/dV images (Fig. 3d-f)

are well reproduced in the corresponding LDOS maps (Fig. 3g-i). The DFT-calculated band

structure (Fig. 3l) reveals that the valence band (VB) is more dispersive than the conduction

band (CB) in the region of around one-third of Brillouin zone edge near the X point, forming

a double-peak structure in the DOS spectrum due to the van Hove singularities at the VB

maximum away from X (peak B') and at the X point (peak C'). In contrast, the bottom of the

CB is significantly flattened in this region of Brillouin zone, forming only one peak in the

DOS spectrum (peak A'). Similar behaviour in electronic band dispersion has been observed

in 6-ZGNR in previous study3. It is also noted that the experimental gap (980 ± 35 meV)

derived from dI/dV spectra is larger than that of the DFT-calculated one (330 meV). Given

DFT's tendency to significantly underestimate quasiparticle bandgaps47 even when factoring

in the screening effects of the underlying Au substrate, it is not surprising that the DFT value

is smaller than the experimentally observed gap. Nevertheless, the relative energy positions

of the three electronic peaks near EF along with their corresponding LDOS, are in good

agreement with experimental data. In addition, our ab initio calculations on 5-ZGNR reveal


<!-- Page 10 -->


that an antiferromagnetic alignment of spins across the ribbon width between

ferromagnetically ordered edge states is favored as the ground state over both the non-

magnetic or a fully ferromagnetic configurations, as illustrated in the spin density plot (the

inset of Fig. 3l; note that the absolute spin orientation is arbitrary due to negligible spin-orbit

interactions in carbon systems).

In striking contrast, our DFT calculations directly demonstrate that the ground state for both

the JGNRs studied is ferromagnetic, with ferromagnetic spin ordered edge states located only

at the intact zigzag edge (inset of Fig. 4h and 4q). As seen in Fig. 4i and 4r, each one of the

originally doubly occupied spin degenerate band splits into a pair of nondegenerate bands

with opposite spin orientation. In particular, near zero energy, the splitted two bands (the

lowest CB and the highest VB) bracketing the EF are edge-state bands and show a splitting

energy gap of 0.21 eV and 0.19 eV for the (4,2)-JGNR and (5,2)-JGNR, respectively. Similar

to the 5-ZGNR, the highest VB of both JGNRs is more dispersive than the lowest CB (which

both are now nondegenerate), forming a double-peak feature (B' and C') in the DOS spectrum

due to the presence of van Hove singularities at the Γ and the X point of the Brillouin zone of

the JGNR. Conversely, the first CB is notably flattened, forming a sharp peak (A') in the

DOS. Despite variations in their widths, the calculated LDOS patterns of these peak states

remain similar, and correspond well with the experimental dI/dV maps. Since the physical

properties of JGNRs near the EF are dominated by these edge states, variations in the JGNR’s

width would only quantitatively change the low-energy physics. According to our prediction

on the (n,m = 2)-JGNR, if the width of the JGNRs goes to infinity, almost all the states in the

lowest CB and the highest VB would be localized at the zigzag edge. However, more bands

will appear near the Fermi level.

Previous tight binding calculations on an infinite width pristine ZGNRs indicate a k-

dependent localization length at the zigzag edge, with states being more localized when

closer to the X point of the ZGNR Brillouin Zone.5 Since the edge states of (n,m =2)-JGNRs

can be viewed as band-folded states of ZGNR, for the peak originating from states near the X

point of the highest VB of JGNR (peak C'), they all originate from states near X point of the

pristine ZGNR. The localization length of those states is small compared to the width of

JGNRs, so the theoretical LDOS pattern shows a localized pattern at the zigzag edge (see Fig.

4g and 4p). In contrast, for states more towards to the Γ point (at near 1/3 way from X to Γ or

beyond), the localization length of those states in the infinite width prinstine ZGNRs exceeds


<!-- Page 11 -->


the width of the JGNRs considered. The corresponding theoretical LDOS pattern (peak B')

shows a delocalized pattern throughout the ribbon width (Fig. 4f and 4o). For the peak

formed by the CB (peak A'), it comprises states from the entire JGNR Brillouin zone, and the

LDOS pattern can be viewed as a mixture of the previous two patterns (Fig. 4e and 4n). We

note that in the experiment, peak B located at near EF for both JGNRs. This is due to the fact

that the work function difference between our GNRs (~ 4.5 eV) and Au(111) (~ 5.3 eV)

entails a charge transfer from the JGNRs to the substrate, which lifts the valence band

maximum upwards to the Fermi level.

## Conclusion

Guided by our topological classification theory, the successful bottom-up synthesis of

atomically precise JGNRs with a single ferromagnetic zigzag edge offers a rich platform not

only for exploring novel quantum spin physics but also for its technological relevance. For

instance, such JGNRs could serve as a model system for realizing ferromagnetic Heisenberg

spin-1/2 chains. Achieving 1D ferromagnetic states in JGNRs also enables the development

of fully spin-polarized current channels. Additionally, the ability to precisely tune the

bandgaps of JGNRs by adjusting their width and edge structure allows for fine control over

band alignment and spin-polarized transport barriers. These features are crucial for advancing

the miniaturization of spintronic devices with enhanced energy efficiency. Furthermore, the

ability to assemble multiple spin centers in 1D JGNRs opens new avenues for creating robust

qubit platforms, leveraging individual π-spins or their collective spin states to achieve

enhanced noise resilience.48

## Method

In-solution and on-surface synthesis. For the synthesis of the precursor of 5-ZGNR, both

branches of the Z-shape precursor are concurrently generated through the Suzuki coupling of

5,5'-dibromo-2,2'-diiodo-1,1'-biphenyl with methylphenyl boronic acid, then generating an

ethynyl group via the cleavage of the triisopropylsilyl. Subsequent PtCl2 catalysed cyclization

of the ethynyl moiety produces two methylphenanthrene motifs connected by a C-C bond

(precursor 3), serving as branches to construct the zigzag edges. In contrast, for the precursor

of JGNRs, one of the two methylphenanthrene branches is substituted by biphenyl and

triphenyl groups by an additional step of Suzuki coupling. The synthetic procedures of the


<!-- Page 12 -->


precursors are detailed in Supplementary Information. Au(111) single crystal (MaTeck

GmbH) was cleaned by multiple cycles of Ar+ sputtering and annealing. Knudsen cell (MBE-

Komponenten GmbH) was used for the deposition of precursor molecules onto clean Au(111)

surfaces under ultrahigh vacuum conditions (base pressure, <2 × 10−10 mbar) for on-surface

synthesis of product 1. The precursor was sublimated at varying temperature for 1 minute to

achieve a moderate coverage on Au(111). After the deposition of precursors, the sample was

stepwise annealed at elevated temperatures as stated in the main text for 20 min to induce

intramolecular dehydrogenation (Fig. S12).

STM/BR-STM/nc-AFM and dI/dV characterization. The experiments were conducted in

Scienta Omicron LT-STM/AFM systems operated under ultrahigh vacuum (base pressure, p

< 2 × 10−11 mbar) at a temperature of T = 4.5 K. All the BR-STM and nc-AFM images were

taken in constant height mode with a CO functionalized tip. The microscope of Scienta

Omicron was equipped with qPlus sensors S0.8 (see table I in ref. 38) with a resonance

frequency of f0 = 39.646K Hz, a stiffness of 3600 N/m, and a quality factor of 119115. nc-

AFM images were collected at a constant-height frequency modulation mode using an

oscillation amplitude of A = 20 pm. The tip-sample distance with respect to an STM set point

is indicated in the figure caption for the corresponding AFM image.The images were

analyzed and processed with Gwyddion software. The dI/dV spectra were collected using a

standard lock-in technique with a modulated frequency of 479 Hz. The modulation voltages

for individual measurements are provided in the corresponding figure captions. The STM tip

was calibrated spectroscopically against the surface state of Au(111) substrate.

Computational Method. First-principles DFT calculations in the LSDA were performed

using the Quantum Espresso packages.49,50 A supercell geometry was employed, with a 10 Å

vacuum spacing placed in all non-periodic directions to prevent interaction between replicas.

The atomic geometry was fully relaxed until all components of the forces on each atom were

smaller than 0.01 eV/Å. A 100 Ry wavefunction energy cut-off, along with scalar relativistic

and norm-conserving pseudopotentials for C and H, were used.51,52

## 1. Theoretical calculations

### 1.1 Z2 index and Z index in GNR systems

The Z2 index is a topological invariant that characterizes the electronic structure of a material.

The Z2 index (0 or 1) distinguishes between trivial and non-trivial topological phases. In the

trivial phase (Z2=0), there are no protected edge states at the interface with vaccum . In

contrast, the non-trivial phase (Z2=1) has robust edge states (or end states in the case of 1D

systems) at the interface with vaccum that are protected against perturbations [1].


<!-- Page 22 -->


However, the Z2 theory requires the system to have time-reversal and spatial symmetry and

does not precisely predict the exact number of protected edge states. To address this, a more

robust topological classification based on chiral symmetry was developed, as chiral symmetry

is a good approximate symmetry for GNR structures [2].

This classification led to the chiral phase index (Z index) for GNRs, where different

topological classes are given by an invariant that is an integer Z. Different Z (which can take

on any integer values) indices correspond to different topological phases. The trivial phase

(Z=0) does not have protected end states at the vacuum/material interface, while the non-

trivial phases (Z≠0) have robust end states. The number of end states is given by the Z index

[2].

### 1.5 Stability of the JGNRs’ electronic structure and magnetism upon charge doping

In the main text, our DFT simulations were done for the JGNRs in the vacuum. However, in

the experiment, the properties of JGNRs were measured on a gold substrate. It is known that

doping and hybridization/screening effects of gold tend to reduce the magnetic order in the

GNRs [3,4]. Therefore, we discuss the effects of charge doping here, demonstrating that the

ferromagnetism and localized spin density of JGNRs remain stable against hole doping and

can survive on a gold substrate.

Since the electronic properties of (4,2)-JGNR and (5,2)-JGNR are similar near the Fermi

level, and charge doping primarily affects the states near the Fermi level, we use (4,2)-JGNR

to illustrate the effect of charge doping. The work function of JGNRs, calculated by DFT, is

around 4.2 eV; therefore, hole doping is expected. Since the work function of a gold surface

can vary depending on the environment, we calculated the electronic structures of JGNRs

under several different hole doping levels and determined the experimental value of hole

doping by matching the theoretical results with experimental results. Fig. S5, S6, and S7

show the band structures, spin densities, and the simulated dI/dV mapping of (4,2)-JGNR

under 0.1, 0.2, and 0.4 holes doping per unit cell. Note that in the experiment, peak B is

consistently around 0.0 eV (with the exact position varying from sample to sample);

therefore, we can estimate that the hole doping level is around 0.1 holes per unit cell.

From the results, we can see that the electronic structure of the system is stable up to 0.2

holes per unit cell. The localized spin density is even more robust against hole doping up to

0.4 holes per unit cell. This is because the states that contribute to the localized spin density

at the zigzag edge are from the first valence band near the X point, which are deeper in the

Fermi Sea and hardly impacted by the doping effect.

# Orbital Engineering Band Degeneracy in a Dual-Square Carbon-Oxide Framework

**Authors:** Fujia Liu; Yuyi Yan; Weichen Tang; Boyu Qie; Jieqi Chen; Ziyi Wang; Steven G Louie; Felix R Fischer

**Affiliations:** †Department of Chemistry, University of California, Berkeley, California 94720, United States | ‡Department of Physics, University of California, Berkeley, California 94720, United States | §Materials Sciences Division, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, California 94720, United States | ∥Kavli Energy NanoScience Institute at the University of California Berkeley and the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, California 94720, United States | ⊥Bakar Institute of Digital Materials for the Planet, Division of Computing, Data Science, and Society, University of California Berkeley, Berkeley, California 94720, United States

## Abstract

Electron band degeneracies in momentum space give rise to exotic quantum phenomena that have sparked intense interest in condensed matter physics and materials science. Nodal-lines—isolines in k-space formed by the incidental touching of two bands that share the same energy but belong to discrete eigenstates—arise in the presence of symmetries that preclude effective hybridization. Despite recent advances in the design, bottom-up assembly, and engineering of exotic electronic states in graphene nanomaterials, the extension of this approach to access synthetic two-dimensional (2D) quantum materials derived from metal- or covalent-organic frameworks (COFs) has lagged behind. Here we present a molecular orbital engineering approach for designing and fabricating an edge-centered dual square lattice within a π-conjugated 2D-tetraoxa[8]circulene (2D-TOC) COF. First-principles calculations and scanning tunnelling spectroscopy reveal the emergence of Frontier states at the center of a 3 × 3 lattice that give rise to Dirac nodal-lines in 2D-TOC. Our findings not only provide a general guide for the design of conjugated COFs with custom tailored electronic properties from molecular fragments but enable the exploration of emergent topological phenomena in synthetic 2D materials with potential application for high-speed, low-power data processing, transmission, and storage.

Keywords: Dirac nodal line semimetal, dual square lattice, orbital engineering, covalent organic framework, Wannier functions

## Introduction

π-Conjugated two-dimensional (2D) covalent-organic frameworks (COFs) have been predicted to host unusual band structures that can give rise to exotic electronic and topological quantum states.1−6 The emergence of magnetism, higher-order topological phases, or (semi)metallicity is intimately linked to the relative arrangement of flat and/or highly dispersive bands near the Fermi level (EF).7−9 Even subtle alterations to the structure and composition of the modular building blocks can lead to dramatic changes to the electronic structure. Efforts targeted at accessing band degeneracies at the Fermi level in COFs remains a vibrant topic of computational studies,10−15 yet despite their highly customizable design, the experimental realization of these theoretical predictions and a systematic exploration of their unusual electronic properties remains broadly unexplored.

Decomposition of the extended electronic structure of 2D COFs into contributions from localized molecular orbitals (LMOs) requires a transformation of the extended periodic Bloch functions.16 Maximally localized Wannier functions (MLWFs) represent a unitary transformation of delocalized Bloch states to a localized Wannier basis17 and offer a physical foundation for a tight-binding (TB) formulation to interpret a material’s band structure in terms of real-space interactions.18,19 The corresponding Hamiltonian can be expressed as

where tRR′nn′ is the hopping parameter of an electron from the nth Wannier function (WF) (derived from a band complex) centered at unit cell R to the n′th WF centered at unit cell R′, εRn is the on-site energy of the WF, and cRn† and cRn are creation and annihilation operators for electrons localized at the corresponding WFs. While this analysis has been used in the past to disentangle structure–function relationships of 2D COFs20−22 (and materials in general), a reverse engineering strategy can be applied to imbue COFs with desirable electronic properties through a modular building block design. An extension of this model to a universal bottom-up approach must account for the hybridization between molecular orbitals (MOs) sharing similar energy levels.

Guided by this idea, we designed a dual-square TB model (i.e., a square lattice with three basis sites) comprised of two superimposed square lattices: the first formed by unoccupied local orbitals on the corner-sites (A-sites) and second involving two occupied orbitals (of different orientation) on the edge-sites (B-sites). The TB model (Figure 1A) is reminiscent of a Lieb lattice, but we impose, by design, that there is no hopping between any edge and corner sites, i.e., tAB = 0, limiting the hybridization and interband mixing near EF.23 Adjusting the nearest-neighbor hopping parameters between A-sites (tAA), between B-sites (tBB), and their respective on-site energies (εA and εB) to εA – 4|tAA| < εB + 4|tBB|, this dual-square model predicts a three-band complex with an intersection of the highest-energy band (with wave function ψA on the A sublattice, nominally the conduction band, CB) and the second highest-energy band (with wave function ψB on the B sublattice, nominally the valence band, VB) at EF (Figure 1B) characteristic for a Dirac nodal-line semimetal (DNLSM).24−33 Theory has suggested that spin–orbit coupling could open a gap that would give rise to nontrivial topological phases in DNLSM COFs.34 To realize a dual-square 2D COFs featuring a DNLSM band crossing, we herein selected molecular building blocks with orthogonal Frontier MOs that satisfy specific phase relationships and energy levels that best approximate the required MLWFs (Figure 1C). To ensure that VB and CB intersect at the desired k-points, the phase of the MLWF at the corner-sites, ψA, and at the edge sites, ψB, must be offset (Δϕ) to place the CB maximum (CBmax) and VB minimum (VBmin) at the Γ point (tAA > 0). Similarly, the wave function associated with the corner-sites, ψA, should be orthogonal (ψA ⊥ ψB) to the edge-sites, ψB, to enforce a symmetry-forbidden hopping that effectively sets tAB = 0.

The stringent conditions imposed by the dual-square TB model can be satisfied in a carbon-oxide framework with p4mm symmetry (Supporting Information Figure S1) based on a tetraoxa[8]circulene (TOC) core fused by cyclobutadienyl linkers (2D-TOC) (Supporting Information Figure S2 shows examples of alternate molecular designs that lead to a lesser or vanishing overlap of VB and CB). Our design employs the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) of tetraoxa[8]circulene (1) as the A-site MO (ψA) and the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) of biphenylene (2) as the B-site MO (ψB) (Figure 1D, complete sets of Frontier MOs for 1 and 2 are depicted in Supporting Information Figure S3). ψA exhibits the symmetry requirement for tAA > 0 and is orthogonal to ψB to minimize hybridization. The validity of this general molecular orbital engineering approach is supported by the evaluation of the overlap integral S = |⟨ψMO|ψMLWF⟩| (ψMO is the normalized HOMO/LUMO wave functions, ψMLWF is the normalized MLWF localized at the corresponding lattice site). The analysis shows that the specific orbital symmetry, relative phase, and energy alignment of ψA and ψB in the 2D-TOC framework is faithfully reproduced by the ψLUMO and ψHOMO of 1 and 2 (SA = 0.89 and SB = 0.75 in Supporting Information Figure S4) ensuring a band crossing that gives rise to a DNLSM.

## Results/Discussion

### Synthesis of Molecular Precursors and Surface-Assisted Growth of 2D-TOC

The design and synthesis of molecular building block 3 that enables the reticular growth of 2D-TOC is depicted in Figure 2A. Tetramerization of tert-butyl-1,4-benzoquinone (4) with BF3·Et2O followed by catalytic cleavage of the tert-butyl groups yielded the parent tetraoxa[8]circulene (1) in 20% yield over two steps.35 Treatment of 1 with elemental bromine gave the reticular building block for 2D-TOC, perbromotetraphenyleno[1,16-bcd:4,5-b′c′d′:8,9-b″c″d″:12,13-b′″c′″d′″]tetrafuran (3), in 86% yield. On-surface bimolecular Ullmann-type coupling36 between vicinal dibromides lining all four edges of 3 gives rise to the cyclobutadienyl fused linkers that span the square lattice of 2D-TOC (Figure 2B).37−39

TOC–COFs were grown on Au(111)/mica films by sublimation of 3 in ultrahigh vacuum (UHV) onto a clean Au(111) surface held at T = 298 K. Figure 2C and Supporting Information Figure S5B–D show representative constant-current scanning tunnelling microscopy (STM) topographic images of closely packed self-assembled islands of 3 on Au(111) at T = 4.5 K. Molecule-decorated surfaces were gradually annealed to T = 643 K (2 K min–1) to induce the homolytic cleavage of C–Br bonds followed by the Ullmann-type coupling of 3. STM topographic images revealed networks of 1D-TOC chains and quasi 2D-TOC (q2D-TOC) ladder polymers intermixed with small patches of 2D-TOC frameworks (Figure 2D, Supporting Information Figure S5H–I) terminated by H atoms along their edges. We attribute the formation of 1D chains and quasi-2D TOCs to the quenching of carbon centered radicals by residual traces of hydrogen atoms generated by the high-voltage ion gauge in the UHV chamber, a process that results in C–H bond formation and termination of surface stabilize radical.40 BRSTM imaging with CO-functionalized tips corroborated the formation of the expected TOC framework (Figure 2E, Supporting Information Figure S5J). Closer inspection of a 2 × 2 cell (Figure 2F) reveals the characteristic p4mm symmetry of 2D-TOC COFs. Four tetraoxa[8]circulene cores are fused into a square lattice along their edges by cyclobutadienyl linkers (lattice constants: a = b = 0.97 ± 0.03 nm; α = β = 90°). Further annealing of 2D-TOC samples to T ∼ 800 K does not result in noticeable decomposition (Supporting Information Figure S5K–M). The unusual thermal stability of 2D-TOC is attributed to the design of the molecular precursor 3 devoid of labile C–H bonds, precluding uncontrolled dehydrogenation and C–C cross-linking, a common side reaction at elevated temperatures.

For comparative analysis, we sublimated the unsubstituted tetraoxa[8]circulene 1, a molecular model for a 0D-TOC (Figure 2B), onto Au(111) using similar UHV deposition methods. Topographic STM images reveal that 1 forms a densely packed monolayer of p4 symmetry (Supporting Information Figure S6A,B), distinct from the assembly pattern of 3 (Figure 2C). BRSTM imaging suggest that the self-assembly of 1 on Au(111) is driven by weak C–H···O hydrogen bonding interactions between tetraoxa[8]circulene cores (Supporting Information Figure S6C,D).

### Electronic Structure Characterization of 0D-, 1D-, and 2D-TOC COFs

We characterized the local electronic structure of 0D-, 1D-, and 2D-TOC frameworks using scanning tunnelling spectroscopy (STS). Differential conductance point spectroscopy of 0D-TOC recorded at the position marked in the inset (Figure 3A) shows a broad gap bracketed on either side by a shoulder, feature 1 (Vs = +1.90 ± 0.05 V) and feature 2 (Vs = −1.70 ± 0.05 V), respectively. dI/dV maps recorded at a bias of Vs = +1.90 V (feature 1, Figure 3B) show a characteristic nodal pattern reminiscent of a checkerboard superimposed on the position of the 8-membered ring. In contrast, dI/dV maps recorded over a narrow bias window around −1.65 V < Vs < −1.75 V (feature 2, Figure 3C) show a distinctive cross-shaped pattern centered on the tetraoxa[8]circulene core and the surrounding benzene rings. At slightly more negative biases, Vs = −1.85 V (feature 3, Figure 3D), this cross-shaped feature broadens to include larger contributions from the oxygen atoms. Experimental dI/dV maps of 0D-TOC are faithfully reproduced by theoretical calculations based on ab initio density functional theory (DFT) within the local density approximation (LDA). Projections of the local density of states (LDOS) of the LUMO (Figure 3E) of 1 mirror the checkerboard pattern seen in dI/dV maps recorded at biases close to feature 1. Similarly, the calculated LDOS of the HOMO (Figure 3F) and HOMO–1 (Figure 3G) are in good agreement with the experimental dI/dV maps of feature 2 and 3, respectively. Excellent correspondence between theoretical LDOS and differential conductance maps suggests an experimental HOMO–LUMO gap of ΔEg,0D ∼ 3.6 eV for 0D-TOC on Au(111).

To extend the electronic structure of TOC frameworks to higher dimensions, we recorded dI/dV point spectra on a 1D-TOC chain containing five TOC units at the positions marked in the inset (Figure 4A). Three prominent features, a shoulder at Vs = +1.07 ± 0.05 V (feature 4) and two adjacent peaks at Vs = −0.85 ± 0.05 V (feature 5) and Vs = −1.05 ± 0.05 V (feature 6) bracket EF. Differential conductance maps recorded at a bias corresponding to feature 4 (Figure 4B) show the signature checkerboard pattern previously associated with the LUMO of 1 at the center of each 8-membered ring. In contrast dI/dV maps of feature 5 (Figure 4C) and feature 6 (Figure 4D) reveal a distinctive DOS pattern comprised of three bright lobes centered on the cyclobutadienyl linkers lining the backbone of 1D-TOC chains. Signal intensity centered on the 8-membered ring gradually decreases with a shift to lower bias. Projections of the DFT calculated LDOS at energies corresponding to the bottom of the conduction band (CB at k = X, Figure 4e), the top (VB at k = X, Figure 4f) and the bottom (VB at k = Γ, Figure 4g) of the valence band (VB) are in good agreement with experimental dI/dV maps of feature 4, 5, and 6, respectively. An effective truncated Hamiltonian constructed in the Wannier basis using a tight binding (TB) model built from two alternating basis states (A-site and B-site) coupled via nearest-neighbor (NN) (tAB = 0) and next-nearest-neighbor (NNN) (tAA = 0.27 eV, tBB = −0.10 eV) electronic hopping parameters (on-site energies εA = 0.76 eV and εB = −0.51 eV) faithfully reproduces the Frontier bands predicted by DFT (Figure 4H). The robust correlation between experiment and theory suggests that 1D-TOC chains on Au(111) are semiconductors with an experimental direct band gap of ΔEg,1D ∼ 1.9 eV. A sizable reduction of the gap by 1.7 eV upon moving from 1 to 1D-TOC chains is fully consistent with an extension of the effective conjugation length across the cyclobutadienyl linkers.

To access the electronic structure of 2D-TOC COFs we collected dI/dV point spectra on a finite lattice comprised of nine tetraoxa[8]circulene arranged into a 3 × 3 square (Figure 5A). Differential conductance spectra recorded at or near the center of the lattice show five characteristic features. The intensities of a broad peak at Vs = +0.65 ± 0.15 V (feature 7), the onset of a shoulder at negative bias Vs = −0.40 ± 0.10 V (feature 10), and a broadened feature centered at Vs = −1.4 ± 0.20 V (feature 11) vary only slightly with tip position. In contrast, the most striking spectral signature, a pair of peaks at Vs = +0.08 ± 0.03 V (feature 8) and Vs = −0.07 ± 0.03 V (feature 9) bracketing EF, can only be observed if the tip is placed above the central TOC in the 3 × 3 lattice. Differential conductance maps recorded at biases corresponding to feature 7 (Figure 5B and Supporting Information Figure S7) show the distinctive checkerboard pattern previously associated with the LUMO of 1 (Figure 3B) or the CB of 1D-TOC (Figure 4B). Signal intensity is largest above the central TOC but spreads across the framework and even persists in maps recorded at Vs = +1.40 V, suggestive of a highly dispersive band. dI/dV maps recorded at the onset of feature 10 (Figure 5C and Supporting Information Figure S7), reveal the signature of a delocalized wave function characterized by three bright lobes centered on the cyclobutadienyl linkers. The dI/dV signal is most prominent at the center of the 3 × 3 square (−0.50 V < Vs < −0.30 V) and shows the familiar cross-shaped feature associated with the 8-membered ring in the HOMO of 1 (Figure 3C) and the VB in 1D-TOC (Figure 4C). The same nodal patterns are preserved across a wide range of biases (−1.50 V < Vs < −0.50 V) spanning feature 11 (Figure 5D and Supporting Information Figure S7) modulated only by a gradual decrease in signal intensity at the core of TOCs (see similar trend in HOMO–1 of 1 in Figure 3D). In stark contrast, dI/dV maps recorded across a bias range straddling EF (−0.20 V < Vs < +0.20 V), bounded on either side by feature 8 and 9, only exhibit a diffuse nodal pattern reminiscent of molecular bonding seen in low bias BRSTM images (Supporting Information Figure S7).

### First-Principles Electronic Structure Calculation

To gain further insight into the electronic structure of 2D-TOC COFs we performed ab initio DFT–LDA calculations on both a finite model for a 3 × 3 TOC square and the infinite freestanding 2D crystal. While projections of the calculated LDOS corresponding to the LUMO, HOMO, and HOMO–1 of a finite system (Figure 5E–G) are in reasonable agreement with differential conductance maps (feature 7, 10, and 11 in Figure 5B–D), finite-size molecular models neglecting substrate interactions (resulting in discrete molecular energy levels) do not reproduce the experimentally observed, sizable band widths (ΔVs ∼ 1.00 V) and fail to explain the emergence of peaks associated with the observed feature 8 and 9 straddling EF. DFT–LDA calculations for an extended periodic 2D-TOC COF fare significantly better (Figure 5K,L). LDOS projections of the CB at k = X (Figure 5H), a narrow shoulder at +0.5 eV < E–EF < +0.7 eV in an otherwise highly dispersive band, show the distinctive checkerboard pattern prominently featured in dI/dV maps of feature 7 (Figure 5B). The considerable width of the DFT calculated CB, −0.2 eV < E–EF < +1.5 eV, is mirrored by the persistent nodal signatures observed in differential conductance maps ranging as far as Vs = +1.40 V. A similar picture can be drawn for the highest occupied bands. LDOS projections of the VB at −0.4 eV < E–EF < −0.3 eV (Figure 5I) and contributions from VB and VB–1 at −1.2 eV < E–EF < −1.0 eV (Figure 5J), near k = Γ point (where the two valence bands are nearly degenerate), faithfully replicate the characteristic pattern of three bright lobes seen in Figure 5C,D. The combined width of VB and VB–1, −1.5 eV < E–EF < +0.1 eV, is reflected in the sizable broadening and substantial overlap of features 10 and 11. Lastly, the model for an infinite freestanding 2D framework provides a plausible explanation for the emergence of features 8 and 9. DFT–LDA calculations for an extended 2D-TOC COF structure (effective tight binding model for a dual-square lattice in Figure 1A with tAA = 0.23 eV, tBB = 0.17 eV, and tAB = 0.0 eV, and on-site energies εA = 0.57 eV and εB1 = εB2 = −0.65 eV) predict that VB and CB intersect at EF giving rise to a DNLSM (Figure 5L). The DOS associated with the VB maximum and CB minimum at k = M would be reflected in dI/dV maps as step-like features bracketing EF. While the detailed picture of a VB-CB band overlap is only expected for extended 2D frameworks the 3 × 3 TOC square represents the smallest assembly that would conceivably exhibit the emerging signature of a DNLSM band crossing.

To validate our theoretical predictions, we recorded dI/dV point spectra across a narrow bias window from Vs = −0.15 V to Vs = +0.15 V along a line bisecting a 3 × 3 2D-TOC square (Figure 6A and Supporting Information Figure S8). The signature of two characteristic peaks at Vs = +60 mV and Vs = −70 mV, corresponding to features 8 and 9, respectively is strongest when the STM tip is placed close to the center of a 3 × 3 lattice (positions d–f in Figure 6A). Differential conductance maps at the relevant biases (Figure 6B,C) show a bright featureless DOS centered on the 3 × 3 2D-TOC square rather than the predicted nodal pattern for LDOS maps sampled across the calculated VB-CB overlap (Figure 6D). The divergence between experiment and theory can likely be attributed to the reduced sensitivity of constant height STS mapping when probing states that feature large contributions from parallel momentum (k∥) vectors (e.g., states at k = M). The larger effective tunneling decay constant means that states associated with the Dirac nodal-line band crossing at Vs ∼ 0 V are masked by contributions from the bulk BRSTM signal.41−43 dI/dV spectra recorded above TOC units lining the edges and corners of the square only show residual signal intensity that gradually blends into the Au(111) surface state (positions a–c in Figure 6A). Furthermore, dI/dV point spectra recorded on two additional distinct 3 × 3 lattices exhibit similar results, with features 8 and 9 displaying the highest intensity near the center of the 3 × 3 lattice (Supporting Information Figure S9). Notably, STS characterization of quasi-2D TOC ladder polymers comprised of 2 × 3 or 2 × 6 lattices (Supporting Information Figure S10), wherein every TOC unit is placed along an edge or corner site, fail to show the corresponding spectral features close to EF. We conclude that the emergence of features 8 and 9 on the central TOC is tied to its unique position within a 3 × 3 square; the only lattice site where the local chemical and electronic environment closely approximates that of the extended 2D-TOC COF.

## Conclusions

Our results provide direct experimental evidence for the emergence of localized Frontier states straddling the EF at the center of a 3 × 3 TOC structure, a model for the extended 2D-TOC COF, that give rise to the characteristic DNLSM band structure predicted by theory. Molecular orbital engineering approaches guided by the transformation of periodic Bloch wave functions into MLWF not only provide a general strategy to design, assemble, and explore emergent phenomena in 2D-COFs, but give rise to a growing class of synthetic 2D quantum materials featuring highly custom-tailored electronic band structures that expand far beyond the limits of naturally occurring 2D materials properties.

## Methods/Experimental

### Sample Preparation

Atomically clean Au(111) substrates were prepared using alternating Ar+ sputtering and annealing cycles under UHV conditions. Submonolayer coverages of precursor 3 were attained through UHV deposition using a commercial MBE cell evaporator operating at crucible temperatures of 573–623 K for 15 min. Substrate temperatures were then gradually ramped (∼2 K min–1) to 643 K and held for 30 min to induce in situ growth of 2D-TOC.

### STM Measurements

Substrates at each stage of growth (0D-TOC, 1D-TOC, q2D-TOC, and 2D-TOC) were characterized using a commercial OMICRON low-temperature (LT)-STM held at T = 4.5 K using PtIr STM tips. dI/dV measurements were recorded with CO-functionalized STM tips using a lock-in amplifier with a modulation frequency of 455 Hz and a modulation amplitude of VRMS = 10–20 mV. dI/dV point spectra were recorded under open feed-back loop conditions. dI/dV maps were collected under constant height conditions. BRSTM images were obtained by mapping the current signal collected during a constant-height scanning at Vs = −10 mV. Each peak position is based on an average of approximately 5 to 8 spectra, all of which were first calibrated to the Au(111) Shockley surface state. STM images were processed using Gwyddion software.44

### Calculations

For molecular simulation, all density functional theory computations were performed using the Gaussian software package.45 Gas-phase geometry optimization used the B3LYP exchange–correlation functional and the def2-SVP basis set.46 After the geometry optimization, single-point energy calculations with def2-TZVP basis set were performed at the relaxed geometry for ground state energies.47 Orbital information was edited using Multiwfn software.48 For periodic systems, first-principles DFT calculations in the local density approximation (LDA) were performed using the Quantum Espresso package.49,50 We used norm-conserving pseudopotentials51 with a 100 Ry energy cutoff and 0.002 Ry Gaussian broadening. A supercell geometry was employed, with a 10 Å vacuum spacing placed in all nonperiodic directions to prevent interaction between replicas. The structures were first fully relaxed until all components of the force were smaller than 0.01 eV/Å. Band structure calculations were performed using 40 k-points along the periodic directions. We used Wannier90 package52 for acquiring maximally localized Wannier functions (MLWFs) from DFT–LDA results and used PythTB package53 to fit the tight-binding parameters. The isosurface value was set to 8 for plotting the orbitals. DFT code can be downloaded from the Quantum Espresso Web site.54 For this study we used Quantum Espresso version 6.7 for the theoretical calculations. The tight-binding simulation code can be downloaded from the PythTB Web site.53 For this study, we used version 1.8.0 for the tight-binding fitting.
